speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) requested a day or two ago that the correspondence relating to the security pact should be laid on the table of the House. Before the request was made, I had communicated with the British government with respect to the correspondence, asking permission to lay on the table such of the correspondence as there might be no objection to disclosing in public. The Secretary of State for the Colonies has advised me that a white paper containing the correspondence on the security pact was published in Great Britain last week, and that it is being sent by mail and should reach Canada by the middle of next week. The British government is of the opinion that it wTould be of advantage if we could arrange to have the whole of this white paper republished in Canada on its arrival; that it would be better to publish leading documents verbatim in Canada rather than have published various telegrams sent during the last two weeks from which communications persons unfamiliar with the subject might find it difficult to gather the present position. The Secretary of State for the Colonies suggests that we might publish at once the original memorandum communicated by the German Ambassador at Paris to the President of the Council on the 9th February and the note from the British government to the German government on the 16th June, the text of both of those documents having been coded yesterday for transmission. I expect that the messages will arrive to-day and if received in time I shall lay them on the table of the House before the House adjourns. These documents are respectively the first and the last in the white paper, the intervening documents being concerned with communications between the French and British governments regarding the terms of the French reply, the gist of which we have had by telegram. I might say to my right hon. friend that I can appreciate the reasons why the British government would prefer to have copies of the same document laid on the table at Westminster and the table here rather than the telegraphic despatches which have passed to and fro, and which as this message, the contents of which

I have just indicated to the House, states, are but summaries and the gist of the main communications. Let me add, that I would be glad, if my right hon. friend or the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) should wish to see the entire file of the confidential correspondence, to place it at their disposal in the interval.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A communication was received asking whether it would be convenient for Newfoundland delegates to participate in the conference. For reasons that must be perfectly obvious the government felt that as the conference was between the West Indies and Canada and not between Newfoundland and Canada or Newfoundland and the West Indies it was desirable in every way to restrict the conference to the representatives of the two countries immediately concerned. The government informed the Newfoundland authorities that if in any way we could facilitate any conference between themselves and the West Indies which they might wish to have we should be only too happy to do so. But we intimated that it was doubtful whether it would facilitate the business with which we were immediately concerned i)f a third party were introduced into the conference. There was no discourtesy of any kind. On the contrary, there was every indication of a desire to co-qpenate with our friends of Newfoundland.

I have an amendment to
submit, as follows:
That subsection 2 of section 150 be amended by striking out all the words in the second paragraph thereof after the word "weights" in line ten up to and including the word "provides" in the twelfth line, and substituting therefor the following words:
"Only when such grain is shipped to a point at which there is no official grading and no official weighing."
The clause as drafted presumes that all grain leaving a country elevator will go to a terminal point or some place where there are official scales and weighing facilities, but such is not the case. A large trade is carried on in the transfer of grain from one point to another, as in the case of feed, seed and various other things of that nature. The clause as drafted makes no provision for that, and I think the amendment would cover it.
I am sorry that we cannot accept that amendment. The clause has been given a good deal of thought by the committee and should, I think, be adopted. It safeguards the interests of all.

I want to understand this
paragraph. It says:
Where delivery is made into cars on track at the country elevator the bill of lading: (if issued) and an affidavit of weight shall upon request be delivered by
Canada Grain Act

the country elevator to the owner and thereupon the country elevator shall be relieved from further liability for grades and weights.
Then it says:
Except in so far as the " subject to grade and dockage " ticket otherwise provides.
If the grade and the dockage is stated on the ticket, would the country elevator be liable, and if it is not mentioned on the ticket would all liability cease?

The country elevator fills up
a car of wheat as requested by the owner. He is given a grade and he has the right to accept that or reject it. If he wishes to name the elevator to which it shall be shipped he has to assume the responsibility. He may say, "I want that car shipped to Vancouver," but if the country elevator is to be responsible for the grain we feel that it should have some voice as to the elevator in which it is to be placed.

The country elevator may
ship a car of wheat and give an affidavit that it contains so many hundred bushels, but how does the owner know what sort of wheat is being shipped? What protection has he got?

Surely no elevator company
would make an incorrect declaration as to weight. When a miller in eastern Ontario buys a car of grain he accepts the weight of the shipper; it is unloaded at his mill and if he finds a shortage, he files a claim against the railway company. As to grade, under the present system the shipper or the owner of the car has the right to examine the shipment. If he thinks the grade stated by the country elevator is not correct, then he can give instructions that the car be shipped on, but it will have to be shipped on the responsibility of the country elevator; it will be inspected and it will receive the grade that is. declared at the other end.

Will the railway company
accept an affidavit from the elevator operator that there are so many bushels in a car and guarantee to settle for that many bushels at the end of the journey?

I might cite the experience of
the eastern Ontario millers. When a car comes in with a shortage we file a declaration with the railway company, and when we establish our claim we receive a refund for the amount.
How do you establish your claim?
Every claim has to be supported by declaration of the person making the claim.

Is there any official
weighmaster who weighs the wheat into the car?

The eastern Ontario miller
simply weighs it in himslf, and the man weighing it in makes the declaration for the company.
Is there an official weighmaster who weighs it into the car?

No.
Mr, GARDINER: Where do the Ontario millers usually get their wheat from,-the public terminal?
From any elevator, from Fort William when it comes by rail, or when lake and rail, from Georgian bay ports.
In that case there would be an official weighmaster who would weigh the wheat into the car?
At the head of the lakes only, not at the bay ports such as Goderich and Port McNicoll.

There would be quite a difference between getting wheat from the head of the lakes, and a car of wheat shipped out of a country elevator. You would have the official weighmaster weigh the grain at the head of the lakes, whereas in the case of the country elevator the operator would simply give an affidavit. There would be quite a difference between accepting that affidavit by the railway companies, and the certificate of the official weighmaster at the head of the lakes.

A country elevator that made false declarations in regard to weight could not remain in the business. If it were found that anything like this happened once or twice, we would become suspicious, and the Canada Grain Board would investigate the matter at once. I do not think there is the slightest chance of any responsible country elevator making a false declaration as to weight.
What is the present practice under the old act? Does not the elevator company guarantee your weight?
Yes, but it has control of the car right to its destination.
Under the old act. does not the farmer have the right to bill his wheat to any terminal he desires?

I do not pretend to understand all this business the way it is drafted in the act. I do recollect, however.

Canada Grain Act
that the mixers were in the saddle the day this was put in, and because of that I feel like shying away from this a little bit. There is a direct premium here to ship to a mixing elevator, because the weights and grades are guaranteed to anyone who will ship to a mixing elevator. That is a tremendous inducement to ship to a mixing elevator. But there is a proviso just before that, to the effect that weights and grades shall net be guaranteed under certain conditions. I wish somebody would explain this to me. I do not pretend to understand it, but it looks bad to me the way it is.

They have always been
guaranteed by the public terminal
Mr. MOTHER'WELL: It says:
Should a country elevator on the order of the owner deliver the grain at a private terminal elevator approved by the country elevator, the country elevator shall guarantee the grade and weight.
There is an inducement to any man to ship to these mixing elevators, because he can have his grades and weights guaranteed.
It is the same if it goes to a public terminal.
Has the m mister turned against mixing since it carried safely last night?
I have never been in favour of mixing but as I cannot have all my own way in this concern, I try to get as much as I can.
The time to raise a row was last night, not now.
I ihink mixing will kill itself in time, but in the meantime I want to get as many restrictions thrown around it as possible.
Are the weights and grades guaranteed if the shipper ships to a public terminal?
Oh yes.

Suppose a farmer unloads 1,100 bushels of grain at the elevator, and asks that it be put on the track as soon as possible The elevator man puts it in a car on the track and says to the farmer, "What are you doing with it?" "I want this sent to the Mutual Elevator, Fort William," the farmer replies. The elevator operator-it may be the Grain Growers'-may say, "We do not countenance
that elevator. If you ship there, it will be at your own risk as to grade and
12 noon weight." The elevator man assumes no responsibility for the shipment. It is true he will sign an affidavit, but he is not liable. He can load 1,000 bushels into that car, and, of course, it will weigh 1,000 bushels when it gets to its destination. The farmer will say, "I have tickets for 1,100 bushels. The car you shipped out is 100 bushels short." Then the elevator man may say, "I told you you sent it to that terminal at, vour own risk," and the farmer is out tha' 100 bushels. He cannot collect on it from the elevator.

How long would that elevator
continue to remain in business if it did that? It would be impossible for it to stay in business.

I submit they should not
be given the power to do it at all. We should reserve the right to the farmer to designate where his grain should go.

I think the point my hon friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) is making will be evident to the committee, but his statement hardly covers all the facts in connection with it. There are four methods by which a farmer may dispose of his grain:
First, he may sell it by the wagon load to the elevator buyer, in which case his grade and price is established at once. He gets cash tickets and the transaction is closed.
In the next case, he may special bm his grain, that is, secure a bin in the elevator, put his own grain into it, and the identity of that grain is maintained. In order that there may be no juggling with the grain by the elevator operator, provision is made in the law whereby a sample may be taken from each load delivered and placed in a tin receptacle, and the farmer delivering the grain has the key and padlock to that receptacle. He has a right to it if he wants to use it.
The next method is this: The farmer may bring in his grain. Perhaps he cannot get a special bin. He and the elevator operator may agree on the grade of the grain, and a graded storage ticket is issued to him for the weight and grade mutually agreed upon between them. That grain is then binned with grain of a similar grade by the elevator operator.
Another method is open to the farmer when he brings his grain to the elevator. He and the elevator operator may not be able to agree on the grade, so he gets a ticket that is called a "subject to grade" ticket. Provision is made for securing samples of the grain, and the samples are forwarded

Canada Grain Act
to the inspector. The inspector gives an official grading on the sample, and that grading governs the "subject to grade" ticket.

The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has mentioned the case where the seller and the buyer cannot agree as to the grade, and he says that samples of that grain are taken and sent to the inspector. I want to know what they do in the meantime with those loads of grain that are waiting for inspection. It must be mixed with other wheat, and put somewhere else. That provision is not very much use.

I do not think my hon.
friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) has fully considered the matter. If he had, he would have seen the position. In the case where the grade is not agreed upon and a "subject to grade" ticket is issued, the elevator operator takes the grain in and puts it with other grain that he thinks corresponds with it in grade, and he accepts the responsibility. But the actual grade is determined by the sample that is sent to the inspector, and it is the inspector's grading that governs, so far as the price to the fanner is concerned.

In the case of the farmer who brings his wheat to the elevator, and who is not able to agree with the elevator man as to the grade, and takes a "subject to grade" ticket, does he have anything to say as to the quality of the grain with which his grain is mixed?

No, and he does not need
to have that, because the grading given by the official inspector will govern. Consequently he gets the grade that the inspector puts upon his grain.
He can dfemand reinspection.

These are the different
methods by which a fanner may dispose of his grain when he brings it to a country elevator. Now we come to the clause we are considering. When the grain is loaded out on track, the elevator company, under the law, is responsible for delivery at a terminal point, if the farmer so chooses, of the amount of grain and the quality of grain that his tickets call for. The elevator has no option in the matter. If the farmer comes to the elevator and says, "I want my grain-quantity, quality and grade as called for by the ticket you issued to me-delivered at Fort William, then they must deliver that to him at a terminal elevator. The point urged by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie is this: If the farmer wishes, he should have the right to get that grain at a country point; in other words 
he could say to me, "You put my grain in a car at an elevator, the amount that my tickets call for, and the quality, and give it to me and you are done with it." But 1 reply, "I am not done with it at that point-, because I have an interest in it to see tha: it is graded and weighed, in order that my interest in the obligation to you may be protected"; consequently the clause provides that I have a right to say where the grain shall go that I may protect my interest, and that is a fair and just proposal. If the farmer says, " I am going to Send the grain out of the country, to Timbuctoo, or Hong Kong"; I say, "All right, if you are going to do that I will give you an affidavit as to the weight and grade but you relieve me of any further responsibility." Is that not perfectly fair? If the grain legislation did not provide that the country elevator operator had to deliver the grade and weight at the terminal, then the argument of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie would be perfectly legitimate; but it is not legitimate, under the circumstances, because I have certainly an interest in the grain in protecting the grade or the dockage that my operator may have given in the country. For instance, it is put into a bin. The elevator operator at a country point who takes in the grain of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie puts four per cent dockage; it comes down to the inspector, and he says, "That is six per cent dockage." Have I not a direct interest in checking that up with the inspector and seeing that my interest is protected by showing that he has put on too much dockage?

Should there be any difference, so long as a car goes to a point where there is efficient weighing and inspection? Should not the inspection at one point be equal to the inspection at another point, and the same with the weighing?
Not necessarily.

My remarks will be very

I thought perhaps by presenting this matter from a slightly different angle from the way it has been presented it might make it a little more clear. I wanted to point out to the committee that the reason why we asked for this amendment, or the justification for asking to retain the right to send our grain to whatever terminal we wish, can be based upon this assumption; the elevator companies are licensed under the act and for a certain tariff they agree to handle grain. On special bin grain up to the present time they have charged If cents a bushel for handling, but the act provides they may charge 2J cents. Up to the present time the majority of the elevator companies have not accepted that opportunity afforded them in the act, and have not charged the high rate, simply because they wished to send it down to their own elevators at the head of the lakes, manipulate the grain and thereby exact an undue toll. Has he not got the

The hon. member for
Assiniboia has the floor.

Will the hon. member for
Brome visualize this feature: The elevator company at the initial point have built their elevator with the object of handling and transferring a commodity which is offered them, and a tariff is laid down in the act to pay them completely for those services. They are absolutely and entirely paid for the services they perform by the tariff the farmer agrees to pay. What right have they in the commodity? What ownership have they in the property, if they have been paid all the charges for the services they have performed?

If they have put their
money into the enterprise and taken the risk of it being destroyed by the fire, they have the rights that are inherent in private property. There are no people in the world who are more likely in the long run to suffer than farmers of the country by interference with the rights of private property.

The insurance and all other risks are covered by the agreement. When a man comes to w-ork on my farm am I obliged to hand over everything to him? I pay him for the services he performs and he has no right to walk off with my team and wagon. He is paid completely for his services and he is through when he receives his fees-and the elevator in this case has received its fees. I want to say again that if the tariff has not been large enough to make this venture profitable for the elevator campanies, they have not taken advantage of the full amount the tariff permits them to charge, and they can yet take full advantage of it. We are prepared to pay that price. This is not a threat, but I honestly believe if this amendment is not allowed to go through, the country elevators throughout the whole of western Canada will suffer loss amounting to scores of thousands of dollars. The people will go to the loading platform; they will load their grain on the tracks, and they will send their grain away. The elevators are not going to have an opportunity of handling that grain except as the owners of the grain require.

Will the hon. gentleman tell
us whether there is any justification for allowing discrimination as against the producer of
wheat, the one who seeks to send his grain through a private elevator to a terminal elevator or the one who seeks to consign it through the private elevator to the pool? Is there any justification for the discrimination which used to exist under this clause?
In the past the owner of the grain had the right to ship it where he wanted.
Without discrimination.

Yes. There is discrimination at the present time. It is not asked for by the producers of grain. They are prepared to accept what was granted to them in the past in this respect. We have the big interests here trying to persuade the committee-at least that is the effect by the insertion of this clause as it stands-to give them a privilege which is not their right. They have a $17.50 investment in a $1,000 policy and they want to dictate the policy because they have that investment.

What injustice would be
done to the country elevators by allowing the farmer to route the grain wherever he chooses?
There would be no injustice done to the country elevator. The country elevator has received the tariff, the charge, which covers all expenses for performing that service.

If the grain was degraded
and the man was obliged to furnish a different grade of grain or pay the difference, would that not be an injustice?
That is the business of the inspector and the government, the Board of Grain Commissioners.
How can he be saved from that risk?

I think the hon. member is involved in his question. He does not understand the initial elevator proposition. This is a grade, storage ticket or special bin ticket that we are referring to, not what is called street grain. Street grain is the absolute property of the individual who has purchased it. He can send it to a private elevator as he wishes. He can mix it. But we argue that, as regards the grade, storage ticket over which the inspector has jurisdiction and the weighmaster at the other end has jurisdiction, the man who owns that grain should have the right to determine where it goes. It is his big investment. That is all we ask for.
Canada Grain Act

But does the country
elevator man not take a risk?

I submit that the issue before us to-day is not whether or not the farmer shall have the right to say where he will have his grain consigned, because in the past the farmer could have his grain shipped wherever he liked. The grain companies, all these years, so long as there has been a Grain Act and so long as there has been grain in western Canada to be shipped, have accepted this condition and they have made no complaint about it. Why the necessity of all this clamour to-day? It is simply this, that within the last year a new factor has been introduced into the grain marketing business of western Canada, that is the grain pool. The grain interests were sufficiently influential in the committee on Agriculture to slip a joker into this legislation, a club with which they hoped to be able to smash these pools. That is the issue. If there were no pools, this issue would not have arisen at all. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) is president of a grain company. He has never complained of this in the past. He has used some strong language in this chamber to-day intimating that a very grievous injustice would be done to the elevator companies if this amendment were allowed to go through. Why did he not complain of that before? He has been a member of this House for eight years. In those eight years he has not, I will maintain, made one complaint nor suggested that there should be a change in the legislation. This reveals clearly the issue at stake, and that is the existence of the grain pools. That is the issue which we have to face to-day. The hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) made an observation this morning that, I think, is worthy of some attention. He stated that if we got this amendment, the farmers would boycott the local elevators and eventually force them to sell out at twenty-five cents on the dollar.

I did not make that
statement at all.

At least that was the way I understood it. The situation is precisely the opposite. If the clause goes through as it is incorporated in the bill today, it means that the farmer cannot use the elevator for the pool except under serious disabilities. Then he will be forced to boycott the elevator, and the elevator will be left high and dry without any business at all. It is a great deal better to leave the farmer the right to use the elevator for his pool, to 
ship the grain to his pool, and in that case the elevator system will be allowed to live and will be perpetuated. There will be a close, harmonious co-operation between the pool and the elevator. There need be no antagonism between them at all.

On the line of my hon. friend's argument, supposing the farmers asked that the grain be shipped through the country elevator to the terminal at Fort William, and the terminal that belonged to the country elevator did not get enough business to operate, what is going to be the result to the terminal elevator?

I was just coming to
that question. The point is this, whether or not there is a pool, we must have the country elevator and the terminals elevator. Just as soon as the wheat pool takes over most of the grain in a district, it will mean if the farmer wants the elevator and he is not allowed to use it, he will either build another elevator or buy out the one that is there. As long as the elevator companies are prepared to concede to the farmer the right to which he is entitled, to handle his grain through the pool, that elevator can exist. The issue of the tolls, has been raised to-day and it has been pointed out that the elevator companies cannot operate under the present tolls. That is their business. They have been ready in the past to accept the 'grain and to handle it for less than it cost them. Why? Because they were determined to induce the farmers to ship through the elevator rather than load it over the platform, and they were prepared to handle it at less than cost in order to induce the farmers to do that. The farmer has not complained of this except in so far as his interests were prejudiced because, when they got the grain, they were able to mix it and make more out of it somewhere else. This is like the freight rate issue. If the farmer has his gTain handled through the elevator for less than the cost of handling, the elevator company must get something out of it in some other way. This is what the farmer has complained of in the past. If the elevators find they cannot operate under the present, charges, the farmer will be the first one to suggest that they raise the charges. I believe the largest elevator company in western Canada, the Saskatchewan Co-operative Company, is charging a higher toll to-day. The farmers are not complaining. They appreciate the fact that this elevator company is prepared to put its country elevators on a paying basis and does not expect to make up the difference

Canada Grain Act
at the terminal. The issue before us to-day is not whether or not a farmer can ship his grain through the elevator where he likes. The point is whether this pool is to continue to exist or not; and what was sufficient for the elevators in the past ought to be sufficient for them to-day. Where do our hon. friends from Ontario and from British Columbia stand to-day? I want to point out to those representing rural constituencies in Ontario and British Columbia that this is a live issue in which they should 'be vitally interested. The farmers of Ontario for years have been trying to build up a co-operative enterprise.
And Quebec.

Yes, and British Columbia. The wheat pool of western Canada is the greatest attempt that the farmers of any country in the world have ever made to build up a co-operative enterprise. So far it has been most successful, and the whole issue of co-operation is at stake to-day. If our hon. friends representing rural constituencies in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia are prepared to oppose us on this vote and strike a. blow at, or drive a nail in the coffin of, co-operation, they are digging a grave for their own efforts, for the efforts of their farmers in their own districts. They have to see this in the way we see it, because the whole issue of co-operation is at stake. This other little petty question, whether or not the farmer can ship his grain wherever he likes, is only an incident. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) read some of us a lecture here three years ago when we tried to get a wheat board. He was opposed to paternalistic legislation. He believes in individualism rather than in the sort of thing we are looking for at the present time. If the hon. member is consistent he will assist us in this to-day. He opposed the wheat board-
I opposed a compulsory wheat board and I told you you would do better with the voluntary wheat pool. And you have done better.
Well, we took the hon. gentleman at his word and adopted his suggestion, and now we are trying to make a success of it. Is he going to turn us down?

No one talks more about
even-handed justice than does the hon. member (Mr. Campbell), and no one understands less the principles of justice. He states that the whole existence of the pool depends upon this legislation.
I did not say that the whole existence of the pool depended upon it, but I did say that the matter was of vital importance.

I will not take back the
statement I made. The hon. member said that the existence of the pools depended upon this legislation. Now, if that is so I have a simple question to ask my hon. friend: If the existence of the pools depends upon this legislation, why did not the pools ask it of the Turgeon grain inquiry? The hon. gentleman may search the evidence given before that inquiry from beginning to end-

But they
had the right under the old act.

No, they had not. Hon.
gentleman may search the evidence given before the inquiry from cover to cover, they may read every particle of it, and they will fail to find anywhere any request from the pools, or anyone representing the pools, for this legislation. My hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Gould) states that the farmer has $1,000 of an investment in the grain while the elevator company has only $17.50. That is not correct. If the shipper of grain will take the grain at the country point, well and good. But they do not do that. The law expressly provides that if the owner of the grain so wishes, the elevator operator must deliver that grain at the terminal point and give him not only the weight his ticket calls for but the grade that is on the ticket. But it is unfair to say that the elevator operator has no interest in the grain otherwise. It would perpetrate a rank injustice on any person handling grain through the elevators if any such suggestion as this were adopted. I have always opposed injustice, as I have had the light to see it, and I will continue to do so. I will not support the proposal simply because my hon. friend from Mackenzie or the hon. member for Assiniboia wishes to take a course which in my judgment is not right.
Is the hon. membeT perfectly sure that the farmers had not the privilege before of shipping the grain in this way?

As a matter of fact, I
think there was a doubt under the old act as to whether the farmer had the right or not.
What was the practice?

The grain almost invariably went to the terminal elevator, chosen by the country elevator.
Canada Grain Act

Was any pool grain
handled at that time?

No. Now, some reference was made to street grain. A very large percentage of the grain handled by all country elevators in the arrangement which is made with the pools, is street grain. The farmer may sell his grain that way if he wishes, but the pool manager establishes the spreads between the different grades at which the grain will be bought; and I, operating a country elevator, taking in grain for the pool, have to buy on these spreads. If the grain goes down and my buyer in the country makes an error in judgment and the grain grades less, I have to make good the grade to the pool. That being the case, I come back to the point that I have the right to a say in the destination of the grain and the inspection of it. As to the other question, of the desire of the pools to ship grain to their own terminal elevators, they are acquiring elevators in the prairie provinces at the present time, and they may send wherever they want to, any grain that goes through these elevators. They are entitled to that right in their own interests. Now, if you create a condition of affairs whereby you impose such handicaps upon the country elevator operator that he has to raise his charges in the handling of the grain through the elevators, who will suffer? It is true that the members of the pool may not suffer, but what about the fifty per cent of the farmers, who are outside the pools who may not wish to enter it? You put an injustice on them inasmuch as you increase the cost of handling the commodity. I cannot see the reason or the justice of the amendment proposed and I shall oppose it.

Nothing herein shall prevent the owner of such grain from, at any time before it is shipped to terminals, requiring it to be shipped to any other terminal than as hereinbefore provided.

terminal. This would seem to be covered by subsection (3).

M,r. McTAGGART: I should like the minister to answer the question I have asked him.

I am instructed by the chairman of the board, who is a lawyer by profession, that the clause is very .general. It has been said by a number of gentlemen on the other side thaft under the old act certain rights were provided which are now being taken away; but .the intention of the bill is to dear up a situation that was indefinite under the legislation we have had. Under the old act the farmer could not direct, for example, that his grain should go to Vancouver. Subsection 2 of section 159 of the old aat covers the .point. It provides that:
-the grain is deliverable to the person on whose account it has been taken into store, or to his order, from the country elevator where it was received for storage, or, if either party so desires, in quantities not less than carload lots,-
And so on. The trouble was that the fanner might wish to go to a certain terminal elevator, and the country elevator owner might wish to go to another, and it was to clear up this difficulty that the amendment was introduced. Under the old conditions before the wheat pool the farmers had not the same interest in the terminal elevator as they have today. But the crux of the situation is this, that, as has been stated to-day, the country elevators receive a revenue of If cents a bushel, and therefore their responsibility should be taken over by the farmers if they wish to ship their wheat to any particular terminal elevator.

Is it not a fact that in the past the working out of the act has been such that it did not prevent the farmer from having his grain sent wherever he wished? I am not arguing the legal point, but that is how it has worked out. That, I may say, is the reason why the pools did not raise the question.

It is in order to clear up that
doubtful point that this section is so drafted in the new act.

Canada Gram Act
The minister will admit that they have cleared it up to the disadvantage of the farmer.

I hardly think so. It has been argued that the certificate issued by the country elevator might be a hundred bushels short, but I do not think any country elevator would get away with that type of business for any length of time.
If this is put purely on a moral basis, why have the Grain Act at all? Why not put the whole handling of grain on the same basis if you can trust the honesty of the elevator operator in this case?

We have to have a certain
amount of trust in one another in this world. If the country elevators are to be held responsible for the grain, they should have the right to determine the terminal elevator to which they deliver it. But, if the farmer wishes to assume full responsibility, he has the right to ship his car to any elevator he may designate.

Mr. Chairman, this
seems to be the first clash in this House between the co-operative method of handling grain and the competitive. There are a great many of us in this part of the House who are not lawyers, and I share their view that the new clause will discriminate against the pool, and that that is the purpose of it.
No.

Possibly not, but one
may well wonder why it is inserted in the act, for it was not there before. The pools are a new factor in the marketing of wheat, and as a representative of farmers who are striving after co-operation as their only method of emancipating themeslves from economic oppression, I feel it my duty-and I want to say so in words as well as by vote-to support the western farmer in his effort to get himself out of the grasp of the grain and elevator companies.

Mr. Chairman, I have
hesitated very much about taking part in the discussion because there seems to be a tendency amoilg some of my hon. friends to rather take it for granted that everyone with a viewpoint on this question not absolutely in agreement with the majority has some ulterior motive to serve.
No.

I do not say that in any
offensive spirit, but I rather drew the conclusion from the remarks of some hon. members. I assuredly have no motive to serve
in this discussion because I am not interested in the grain business in any way. Of course, I am interested generally in the handling of grain at the head of the lakes, because it will come there whether from the pool or from the private elevators. There is a side to this question that has been touched upon by the member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and one or two others, but I wish to look at it from another aspect. Most of the country elevators were built by the people who own the private elevators at the head of the lakes as feeders for the latter.

Is it not a fact that the
biggest and probably the first terminals to be built at Port Arthur and Fort William were built by railway companies that did not own a single country elevator?

That is quite correct, but many of those elevators are in the hands of the railway companies no longer. The fact, however, remains, according to my understanding-and I think it is correct that most of these country elevators were built by companies owning elevators at the head of the lakes to take in the gram from the prairie provinces and pass it on to their terminal elevators. That being the case, they have some rights. It seems to me that if you force the country elevator to take in your wheat and then to send it to the terminal elevator of another company, you are doing very much as if you went to the Canadian Pacific, for example, and said, "Here, I want you to load this car for me, but I insist that you hand it over to the Canadian National Railways." There is that side to the question. In other words, if you force the country elevator out of its natural channel in that it was built as a feeder to its terminal elevator, you put it more or less out of business, and you force the owners to do something which they do not wish to do. It would seem to me that the cure for the situation would be that if those interested in the pools are not satisfied to use the country elevator as the elevator which is to ship their grain to its own terminal, then they should build their own country elevators. I say that with the best of intentions and without any desire to get into an argument with the conflicting interests here represented. It would appear to me that those who own the country elevators and the terminal elevators also have some rights as well as the grain growers of the west, and while the bill should be dealt with having the best interests of the grain growers in view, the whole question of private ownership of property should not be ignored.

Canada Grain Act
Does not the farmer pay the full price for the service he gets in the country elevator?

And the country elevator
would probably be able to run in that way, but those who built the country elevator intended it as a feeder for their terminal elevator, and if it is not so used their terminal elevator will go out of business.

Is it not a fact that the
elevators at Fort William are practically filled almost to capacity almost every year?

I think probably that is
true.

And they will be used to
that capacity regardless of what change we may make in this act.

That may be so. At the same time I cannot change my view that those who built the country elevators as feeders to their terminal elevators have just as good claims to be considered by the committee as have the grain growers. I say that with all due deference to my hon. friends.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) both intimated that under the old act the farmer had not the right to send his grain to a terminal elevator that was not used in connection with the elevator into which he loads his grain.

I said that this was hot clear

I find myself in rather a difficulty, and I might almost say, painful position. I have been interested in the United- Grain Growers' Grain Company almost, I think, ever since its inception. The controversy now going
on in the House is a continuation of the old fight which has been waged for about thirty years between the fanner and the different

public utilities for the right of the farmer to do his own business. It is not so long ago since we had to do battle with the Canadian Pacific Railway for the right to 'have a car loaded on the siding. They had given a monopoly of all cars to the elevator companies who would construct on their lands houses of 25,000 bushels capacity, so that the farmer could not load his own car. Mr. Justice Turgeon in his report makes it very plain that in his opinion that right was never challenged. He says:
In this respect, however, care should be taken to see that nothing is done which will prevent the wheat pools' selling agents from taking into their private elevators the grain forwarded by the members of the pools, or by the organizations on behalf of the members. According to the agreement entered into by each producer who joins the pool, the grain remains his own property until solid by the selling agency, and the producers arfj virtually doing their own mixing.
As I have said, I have always exercised this right and it has never been disputed in my case; and I intend in the future, if I cannot continue to assert the same right, to do what I can to persuade my people to load at the platform and leave both the country elevator and the terminal idle. There is no injustice done the country elevator company. The weighmaster at the terminal is the link between the shipper and the elevator company, and it is a link of justice in which both hitherto participated. pany to the effect that the wheat had gone into that car, so that it was collected from the railway company. So far as I can see there is no injustice whatever to fear from this amendment. Mr. McTAG'GART: Mr. Chairman, I desire to move the following amendment to this section:
That all the words between the word "agent" in line twenty-one and the word "shall" in line twenty-three be struck out, and the following substituted therefor, "shall be informed by the railway agent of the allotment to him of a car in good order and condition and"
As amended the section will read:
Each such applicant or agent shall be informed by the railway agent of the allotment to him of a car in good order and condition, and shall within three hours declare his intention and ability to load the said car within the time hereinafter prescribed.

I think, Mr. Chairman, this section is even more important than the section to which we have given so much time this afternoon. I believe that the farmers of western Canada would be millions of dollars ahead if they took more advantage of the loading platform, and it is my opinion that if the grain. pool in western Canada proves to be the success which we hope, the car loading platform will come back into its own once again. I have been loading my grain over the platform for many years, and have found that when the loading platform was used very extensively the farmers encountered this difficulty: about the time the name of a prospective shipper was getting near the top of the list as entitled to a car, he practically had to remain in the town or near the station agent in order to insure getting the car when it was allotted to him, because if he did not happen to be in the vicinity the law did not require the station agent to notify him.

No.
(Bow River) He has only three hours after notification within which to declare his intentino of accepting the car.

I am sure the farmers are just as anxious to get their grain to market as the railway companies are to get the cars loaded. Whether they have forty-eight hours, or twenty-four hours, or a week, to do it, they are under a big expense, and they are going to expedite the work as much as possible. There is a new system growing up in western Canada in regard to the threshing of grain. In former years we used to have the big threshing outfits with a crew of twenty men, capable of threshing from 1,500 to 2,000 bushels of grain a day. There is now coming into vogue a smaller machine capable of threshing from 400 to 800 bushels a day, so it

is utterly impossible to load a car of a capacity of 1.000 bushels, to say nothing of a 1,500 bushel car, in twenty-four hours. It will not affect my district because most of our threshing is done in August, but further west where the seasons are later it may make a difference to the farmers if they are competed to pay demurrage on cars that are held over twenty-four hours. Is it not the case that the

If the minister will come

I know the railways are
very much opposed to this. Millions and millions of dollars are spent in getting cars ready to move the grain crop, cars that lie idle for a good part of the year outside of that. This proposal means doubling the time for loading, and practically doubling the number of cars you will have to have to meet the demand. That will be added to the rate on your grain. There is no other way of getting at it. I think hon. gentlemen ought to be satisfied with this bill. We have gone on and not pressed all these things because they might raise opposition in quarters where we do not want to have it raised, but to endeavour to get the railways to double the time in which a car should be loaded is only hampering the whole grain movement, and I think would be of no benefit at all to the farmers themselves.

I agree with the two ministers. I live and market my grain eight and one-half miles from a loading platform, and

with my neighbours' assistance I succeed in loading my car of grain on time, sometimes not within the twenty-four hours, but the railway companies are very generous and they have not been inclined to impose this dollar a day demurrage. Even if they did so, I argue that the farmers is receiving a service at away below cost when he can hold a car another twenty-four hours at the loading platform for one dollar.
In regard to the argument about small machines, if the farmer chooses to use a machine that will thresh only from 400 to 800 bushels a day, why should the railway companies or the neighbours be penalized for that? If the amendment carries, we shall have succeeded in providing for three cars at the loading platform placed side by side or endways, allowing three farmers to load at one time. That has been found necessary because of late years, since the old act was drafted, the cars have increased in size, and we have found that three men could not load at one time. But this new provision regarding the loading platform is going to be the greatest factor in shipping grain from western points in future, and so far as I am concerned I am not going to press for anything further than the act gives us at the present time.

I was speaking a few

I load my grain over the

Like my hon. friend (Mr. Gould) I have never found the railway trouble me very much about demurrage. That is my experience. I opposed this amendment

Right Hon, ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):	Mr. Speaker, what an
extraordinary state of affaire! The government. has read out from the Chair a long series of resolutions involving its view of constitutional doctrine, and the application of that doctrine in respect of a variety of amendments made by the Senate to a bill, and the House is invited to vote upon it without the slightest exposition of the principles, without any explanation even of the Senate amendments, with no discussion as to the relation of the principles to the amendments-indeed, without a word from the government at all. In the first place, I do not think the government should ask the House to even discuss the matter now-
We are not.
-without adequate preparation. But to suggest, as I observed hon. members did, that the House vote upon it without discussion, is to me an affront to parliament.
May I ask the government whether, in regard to the unfortunate few that are now permited under the Senate amendments to receive relief, we are by this motion depriving them of that relief?
Probably.
Is this action of the government simply assisting the Senate to destroy the last vestige of hope for the depositors?

No, it is not
that at all.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?

Is this matter to be put to a vote of this House in a manner such as this? It is unheard of. Does nobody on the government side know anything about it? Are we to have no explanation or exposition at all? I suggest that we have an exposition and that the matter be postponed until hon. members have had an opportunity to review any merits there may be in it. But we should have an exposition now from the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not understand the attitude taken by my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). He claims that the government should define what its policy is in regard to this matter. Well, the very words of the resolution enunciate the principles on which the government base its refusal to accept the amendments of the Senate. If my right hon. friend objects to that declaration of principle, he is at liberty to discuss it as long as he likes. I do not see what affront is being made to parliament by this resolution. So far as the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) are concerned, I may say that this is going to the Senate and the Senate will have to declare whether or not they insist on their amendments. If they insist on their amendments they will send a message to this House stating so, and this

Home Bank
House will then be at liberty to ask for a conference with the Senate with a view to coming to some understanding. Then it will be time to decide what the ultimate course will be and whether the bill is to be accepted as amended or altogether destroyed.

It seems to me that we can never get away from what appears to be a rather melancholy position in connection with the Home Bank case. We are familiar with the start. We are familiar with how the investigation started. The first order in council, we know, was a purely political affair, so much so that it could not stand and was amended. Then again we had a political discussion in connection with something which should not have been a political discussion. We should be able to assume that the House was in earnest and wanted to do something for the depositors. We had a matter brought up in connection with a letter read by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) from Senator Robertson. We had in the first instance the case of a Conservative ex-Minister of Finance. We have in the next instance the suggestion-yes, more than a suggestion- that unless the amount provided for in the bill was placed in the estimates there would be a danger of the Senate doing exactly what it has done. The House could be assumed to be earnest and serious in its legislation: it could be assumed to mean what it said when last year it declared that irrespective of what happened not a cent of contribution could be made in eases of this kind. We are always losing sight of what we ought to have before us in connection with this case, namely, the needs of many needy people. But to-day this is to be lost sight of because we have to make a declaration of independence of this House as against the Senate. This constitutional fight may interest the on-lookers but I do not know what is to become of the claims of the depositors in the meantime. They will get nothing, or they will have to wait until we reach the end of this constitutional struggle. This motion does not ask for a conference; it is a notification to the Senate that the Senate have acted outside of their powers and that the course they have taken is entirely nugatory. It is an extraordinary fact that government members in the Senate took part in these proceedings and supported the action taken; that a member of the administration in the Senate supported it.
Hear, hear.
A Greek chorus. .
I beg my hon. friend's pardon?
I did not mean to interrupt, but I was commenting on the "hear, hears" from the leader of the opposition. It was just like a Greek chorus.

My hon. friend may laugh, but this is a serious matter. A great many people are in a very difficult position as a result of the failure of the Home Bank. My view is just what it was when we were discussing the matter before, namely, that the necessitous cases should be looked after; that the measure was one not of indemnity but of relief where relief was needed and where relief was due. My position has been that I would like to see the really necessitous cases paid one hundred cents on the dollar, and that eleemosynary institutions, charitable organizations and things of that character should be treated in the same way. What really astonished me was the statement the Prime Minister made when he dealt with the Robertson letter. Why, it was necessary then, he said, that this matter should go to the Senate not tied to a Supply bill but in such a way that the Senate could deal with it and could function. The Prime Minister made a red hot attack upon Senator Robertson because, forsooth, he had suggested that the appropriation for reimbursement would be attached to the Supply bill, which, as everybody knows, does not raise any constitutional question. Everybody knows that the Commons and the Commons alone have power in the field of everything covered by the Supply bill.

Does my
hon. friend not agree that if the Senate can do what they have done in relation to the Home Bank bill, they could do it also with the Supply bill?

I certainly do
not. The authorities make a sharp distinction between grants in aid of His Majesty, grants of supply, votes for housekeeping expenses, and other matters. Why, Mr. Speaker, can the Senate amend a railway bill to which this government is the endorser? Can they amend the amount of the bonds which they seek to have issued for a branch line? Can they stop it? Can they alter it? Do they not do it every day? But no one as far as I have heard has ever suggested that they had any such right whatever in connection with Supply. There is a very great difference.
Home Bank

But I am not so much concerned to-day about these questions of legal right here and legal right there. If we are sincere in looking after the depositors who need the money, we are not going to do anything which is going to entirely prevent them from getting any relief whatever. In the first instance, was there any way-supposing, for example, the government were not sincere in this; I am not saying they were not, but supposing they were not sincere-was there any way in which the government could put themselves in this position the more readily than by what has been done, putting themselves in the position of saying to the depositors: "We are going to do everything for you,"1 thereby getting their support, and then making sure they would not have to find the money. Supposing the government had not been sincere, what would they have done? Well, they would have put through an act like they put through last year, which would say: Under no circumstances can depositors get a cent, and they would say: That act we put through last year will apply not only in a case like this, but in a case which is far, far more urgent, in a case where neglect is far more outrageous, in a case where we set up the machinery to see these banks are run properly, in a case where negligence can be charged and brought home, but nevertheless under no circumstances can any payment be made at all.
Then again, if they had wanted to make sure it would be thrown out, could they have done better than to keep it out of the Supply bill-on the very grounds urged by the right hon. the Prime Minister in this House, that he was keeping it out of the Supply bill so that the Senate could go fully into it, so that the whole matter could be handled not only by this House but also by the Senate.
Then again, could anything have been more calculated to bring about the result than the use of the letter?
Again, if the idea be that we are to have a fuss about this and no one is to get any money, could that end be better brought about than by now engaging in the dying days of the session in a long discussion. It must be long-hon. gentlemen have heard the grounds read over; they are long enough, and if there is anything in them they are grave enough to merit some discussion. If you want to defeat everything, can you do better at the present stage than to enter upon the discussion which the government now invite the House to enter upon? Is there any surer way of ensuring that the depositors get nothing?

Does my
hon. friend not know that this is the ordinary procedure that has been followed in every case where there has been a disagreement between the two Houses? There is nothing new about it.
I think my hon. friend is wrong there.
Not at all.

My hon. friend will find that when we really want to get something done, the way is not to decorate our coats with quite as many chips as this, but to ask in the first instance for a conference, and see if the matter cannot be arranged.
No.
This is the ordinary procedure.

Hon. gentlemen say no. Well, if they had put their protest not on the ground of all these various rights, which may or may not be correct, but on the ground of the necessities of indigent depositors that would be a very different thing indeed.
