riiOPOSED PAYMENT OF DEPOSITORS TO THE AMOUNT OF $5,450,000

The House resumed consideration of the motion by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for non-concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 182 for the relief of the depositors of the Home Bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker,
when the House rose for adjournment I had been discussing one or two phases of this question, and among others the attitude taken by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister when he was defending the course adopted by his government in introducing a bill instead of a vote in Supply for the relief of the Home Bank depositors. At that time there was no doubt at all in the mind of the right hon. gentleman that there was of necessity a very great difference between Supply and a bill in relation to the Senate jurisdiction and right to affect our legislation. As reported at page 4219 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
With regard to a measure of this kind which affects all classes in this country, it is of the utmost importance that it should be presented in the form of a bill. Indeed, if this government had denied the Senate the right of discussing this measure, what stronger weapon against any Senate reform would :t have been possible to have placed in the hands of those who would like to see the Senate in its powers remain as it is?
I pause at that point to wonder whether the move now made is to form item No. 1 of the agenda of next year's conference on the powers of the Senate. Apparently the right hon. gentleman thinks the Senate has the right to look after matters of this kind, but if it has not, if it is innocuous, if it is without power, he goes on:
What stronger weapon against any Senate reform would it have been possible to have placed in the hands of those who would like to see the Senate m its powers remain as it is? The people as a whole have certain rights which should be conserved, not only in this House but in the Senate as well. It is only when the Senate by its action repeated over and ovei again obviously defeats what is the will of parliament, that the Senate's action in any essential particular should be controlled. Once again I wish to say that the government has brought in this measure in the form that it has so that there would be no room for criticism on the part of hon. members opposite, either as to the method of bringing about this relief, or as to the fairness of the method by which the government has proceeded-
There was no secret as to what was the right way to bring it about, and in so far at any rate as one of the leading members of the Senate was concerned, he had pointed out that the proper procedure was to put in
our Supply bill a vote to cover the amount of relief to be granted to the depositors. So I can hardly think my right hon. friend was serious in making those remarks. But the government thep recognized the difference in the procedure, and recognized the right of the Senate to amend this bill.
Now, I am not going to argue whether the Senate is right or wrong I am concerned to see that the question of relief to the Home Bank depositors is not held over for this conference or because of the constitutional fight in connection with the matter. I am only going to assure hon. gentlemen that this is nothing new. Of course, so far as the matter of practice is concerned we know a good deal about it. We know, for example, that lean bills in connection with the railways have been considered, and have been changed by the Senate. We know that with regard, not to one but many railway bills the recommendation of this House has been entirely changed by the Senate. But in all those cases no protest was made at all by the government. It may be that what the Senate did was without right. We have a rule of the House which proclaims very definitely the position of this House, we have also the position taken by the Senate, and, further, we have the provisions of the British North America Act.
Now, so that hon. gentlemen will understand the magnitude of the controversy which is provoked, and in the maze of which I am afraid the Home Bank depositors are going to be lost altogether, I refer them to the Minutes and Proceedings of the Senate of May 15, 1919. They will find at page 422 a carefully prepared memorandum on the rights of the Senate in matters of financial legislation. They will also find that the memorandum-which is lengthy, and which I am not going to trouble the House by going over in detail-was submitted to constitutional lawyers. They will find the considered opinion of Mr. Lafleur, in which he is joined by Mr. Geoffrion, at page 429. The opinion is carefully drawn, and reasons are given. It winds up by saying:
Under the circumstances, we are of the opinion that the Senate of Canada may amend-

If my hon. friend will
allow me, according to rule 16, paragraph 203 of , Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, allusions to debates in the other House are out of order. It says further:
There are few orders more important than this for the conduct of debate and for observing courtesy between Houses.
Home Bank

Sir HENR.Y DRAYTON: May I point out to my hon. friend that as yet Mr. Eugene Lafleur and Mr. Aime Geoffrion are not senators. What I am reading from is a considered opinion given by these gentlemen, I am reading, it is true, from a record, but I am not reading part of a debate.

I will call the attention
of Mr. Speaker to rule 16, paragraph 202 of Beauchesne, which says:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the House and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the House.

I am not even
within radio broadcasting distance of that point, Mr. Speaker.

I understand the hon
member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) is citing two legal authorities on the respective powers or jurisdictions of the Senate and the House of Commons as regards money bills. I happen to have read the opinion in question. It is not part of a debate which took place in the Senate. It is a document contained in the report of a special committee of the Senate. Any constitutional authority can be quoted in the House, whether the name is Lafleur or Geoffrion, whether it is May or Bourinot, or anybody else. As regards the first objection made by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) it would be an objection to be considered if the hon. member for West York were commenting on views held by senators. But the very question now before the House is the issue which has been raised as between the Senate and the House of Commons with regard to the power to amend money bills. Therefore, the remarks of the hon. member for West York are pertinent and I do not think that the hon. member should insist on his objection.

Mr. Speaker, I
am not going to give the whole of this opinion. It would be helpful to do so, but I do not want to delay the House. I will simply point out the conclusion. It says:
Under the circumstances, we are of the opinion that the Senate of Canada may amend a money bill originating in the House of Commons as fully as the House of Commons can do. Of course the powers of the Senate are limited to the same extent as those of the House of Commons by the fact that money bills must be recommended by a message of the Governor General.
But the opinion is not all on one side, Mr. Speaker. I am only pointing out the difficulty that is ahead of us if we are really going to tackle the question this session, before we can do anything about the Home

Bank depositors. There is another opinion given, that of Mr. John S. Ewart. He does not state it quite so categorically, but the gist of his conclusion is that the Senate is without that power.
Where is it to be found?

It is to be found at page 431 of the Minutes of Proceedings of the Senate, of date May 15, 1918. The memorandum draws a clear distinction between a money bill of this character-that is, a money bill -which is not for the granting of supply to His Majesty, but for an entirely different purpose-and a bill which has to do with the requirements of the public service. The memorandum recognizes the absolute right of the Commons to secure its supply.

Has that opinion been
laid on the table of the House of Commons?

I am afraid I
cannot tell my hon. friend whether it has or not.

Well, if it has not, I rise to another point of order. Rule 19 refers to the discussion of messages or reports which are not regularly before the House. That document is not before the House. How can we follow the hon. gentleman's argument when he quotes from a document which is not before us?

It is not necessary to say anything in answer to that. If that principle were followed, it would be impossible to quote from a statute without first laying it before the House. It would be impossible to quote from anything without first laying it before the House.
The statutes are public.

My hon. friend
gets a little mixed as between a report in connection with the business of the House, on which this House has to act, and the statements of outside authorities, to which we certainly can refer. Anyway, the hon. member is a little bit late in starting. I had finished with the opinions; there they are.

I would like to have a
decision from the Speaker first.

I thought I had given a
ruling. In my humble judgment there is no point of order. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) is simply citing the opinion of two legal gentlemen on the respective powers of the Senate and the House of Commons as regards money bills. The point would be well taken if he were citing

Home Bank
from a document emanating from the Senate which had not been laid on the table of the House of Commons. Bourinot, of course, has never been tabled, May has never been tabled. They are authorities on parliamentary usuage and customs and procedure. The hon. member for West York is quoting the opinions of two legal gentlemen regarding the question at issue.

Without discussing your
decision, Mr. Speaker, with your permission may I say that a distinction should be made between the law and private commentaries on the law. Laws are public, and documents which are private have to be laid before the House before they can be discussed. Otherwise other members have absolutely no power to control what the members quoting these documents may say.

The hon. member for
West York is not quoting from a document emanating from the other House. He is citing the opinions of two legal luminaries as regards the question at issue. Whether they give their opinion to members of the upper chamber, or to members of the lower chamber, matters not. Their opinion is simply cited to add weight to an argument.

I have been
absolutely fair in giving opinions both ways, so some of them at any rate must be worth something. At all events they constitute a valuable contribution to anything that may be said upon this subject, if hon. gentlemen want to look the subject up, frankly L do not want anybody to. have to look the question up. I want to see some action one way or the other on its merits, if the government so desires, in connection with the Senate legislation. There is no question on the merits of these points at all. These points are entirely legal. I simply again point out that if we are to go into a legal fight in connection with this matter, if we are to consider the preparation of ammunition for a campaign against the Senate, the rights of the depositors of the bank most assuredly are going to suffer.

The hon. gentleman who has just
resumed his seat (Sir Henry Drayton) has stated that he wants action. May I point out to him and to the House that the only way in which action can be taken at this stage, consistent with what the House has already done, is precisely the way in which the House is asked to proceed by the motion which has been placed in your hands, Mr. Speaker. In no other way at the present stage can 'action be taken.
A brief recital of the facts may help to clarify the situation, and at the same time make plain to the hon. members 9 p.m. of this House that the government is acting strictly in accordance with the procedure that is applicable to cases of this kind, and that there is nothing irregular or unusual about what has been done, or about what is proposed to be done. Let us look at what has happened.
On the 10th of June this House passed a bill, No. 182, An Act for the relief of the depositors of the Home Bank of Canada. As so passed, that bill was then sent to the Senate. The Senate in the exercise of its wisdom not only amended that bill, but, in effect, drafted an entirely new bill. So that there may not be any doubt on that subject let me quote an authority which will be accepted not only by hon. members of this House, but also by members of the other branch of this parliament.
Has the authority been tabled?

It is in the reading room of the Commons. The editor of the Montreal Gazette is also a respected member of the Senate, and in his paper of the 22nd of June there is an editorial, part of which is as follows:
The new or revised Home Bank bill as sent to the House of Commons by the Senate is a notable example of skilful legislating. In the first place, the dangerous principle of compensation and the poor pretence of a moral obligation is rejected, the bill being thereby purged of its essentially vicious feature.
A little later on the editorial says:
There is virtually a new bill which provides for a distribution upon an entirely different basis and to a more limited extent, and even the title of the measure has been changed.
Still later on in the same editorial in the Montreal Gazette, the owner of which, as I have stated, is a respected member of the Senate, there is this statement:
The "moral responsibility" basis is formally repudiated in the legislation.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a very apt description of what took place in the Senate. After that had been done, the Senate sent the bill back to this House. The situation then was that this House had either to concur in the amendments that had been made, or rather accept this entirely mew bill drafted by the Senate, or disagree to the amendments. The government proposes that this House will not concur in these amendments, or accept this new bill, and the government has stated its reasons for taking that attitude in the motion which has been placed in your hands,
Home Bank

Mr. Speaker. That, Sir, is entirely in accordance with the regular procedure in such cases.
Now what is the further procedure that is to be taken? My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) briefly stated that further procedure this afternoon. Allow me to briefly re-state it.
As I have said, the reasons for the action proposed by the government are fully set forth in the motion before us. Now under the rules and procedure and the precedents recognized in this House, the further steps to be taken may be briefly summarized as follows: Assuming that the motion in your hands, Mr. Speaker, would pass, then a message would be sent to the Senate. That is the usual course. The message in all these cases is such as you have read to the House, or one similar to it applicable to the circumstances of each case. Having received that message, the Senate then agrees to the position taken by the Commons, or disagrees. If the Senate agrees, then the matter under discussion is easily adjusted. If, on the other hand, the Senate disagrees or insists upon its amendments, it sends back a message to the Commons to that effect. Having received that message, this House then asks for a free conference with the Senate. If the Senate agrees to a free conference, this House names its representatives, or, as they are called under parliamentary procedure, the managers, who will represent it at the conference. The Senate names its managers, and1 the conference takes place. Now it is only when that conference has taken place that the. ultimate fate of this bill can be determined, and it is only when that conference has taken place that an answer can be given to the question that was asked this afternoon by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland), and I think by another hon. member of the House. Therefore the motion that has been placed in your hands, Mr. Speaker, is the first step towards the action which my hon. friend the member for West York desires should be taken.
As I have said the reasons for the government's position are fully set out in the motion in your hands, Mr. Speaker. This afternoon there was some intimation given that this action was not supported by authority. With that statement I join issue, and in support of the position taken by the government I quote Bourinot. At page 444 he says:
The House of Commons alone has the constitutional right to initiate measures for the imposition of taxes and the expenditure of public money.
Section 53 of the British North America
Act says:

Bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue, or for imposing any tax or impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
And further, in the speech with which the Governor General opens and closes every session of parliament, he recognizes the constitutional privileges of the House of Commons with respect to the estimates and supply, for he addresses its members only with respect to these matters. Thus is the position of the government supported by Bourinot. I desire to quote Todd on the same point at page 476 That author in comparing New Zealand and Canadian legislation, proceeds to speak thus:
But neither the New Zealand nor the Canadian laws can be so construed as to warrant a claim by the upper chambers of either parliament to equal rights in matters of aid and supply to those which are enjoyed and exercised by the Commons House of Parliament of the United Kingdom; for such a claim, if insisted upon, would, to a like extent, derogate from and diminish the constitutional rights of the representative chamber.
And he proceeds further:
The Victorian Constitution Act, 1865. section 56. and the British North America Act, 1867, section 53, severally declare that bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue-
Not merely Supply bills, but bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue or for imposing any tax or impost, shall originate in the House of Assembly or the House of Commons.
No further definition of the relative powers of the two houses is ordinarily made by any statute. But constitutional practice goes much farther than this. It justifies the claim of the imperial House of Commons (and by parity of reasoning, of all representative chambers framed after the model of that House), to a general control over public revenue and expenditure, a control -which has been authoritatively defined in the following words: All aids and supplies, and aids to His Majesty in parliament, are the sole gift of the Commons, and it is the undoubted and sole right of the Commons to direct, limit and appoint in such bills the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which ought not to be changed or altered by the House of Lords.
And that last statement is recognized as a great parliamentary principle, and it has been
adopted practically in all self-governing British parliaments, and it forms part of the standing rules of this House. Rule 78 says:
All aids and supplies granted to His Majesty by the parliament of Canada, are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the House, as it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, wheb are not alterable by the Senate.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I cite further the authority of Redlich. That author at page 119 says:
All taxes, duties and grants of money, and all measures imposing financial burdens on the people are matters within the sole jurisdiction of the House of Commons;

Home Bank
He further says:
Closely connected with the first of the Commons' rights in money matters is a second, inseparable from it and equally fundamental. They are entitled to order and dispose how the national revenue, whether permanent or annually granted, is to be spent, and to do so in the greatest detail.
Then at page 120 the same author says:
Both income and expenditure are therefore completely and exclusively in the hands of the House of Commons.
At page 122 there is a further declaration:
The crown alone, or to speak more accurately the government alone, has the right to ask for public money for definite purposes or to propose to the House the expenditure in a definite way of moneys already granted.
Some question has arisen as to the character of this measure, and doubt might therefore have been raised in some minds as to whether or not it is a money bill in the proper acceptation of that term. I find in May's Parliamentary Practice, page 574, a definition of a money bill taken from a resolution of the British House of Commons, and as we know this parliament follows British parliamentary practice, I submit that resolution applies with equal force to money bills of this parliament. At page 574, May says:
For the purpose of this resolution a bill shall be considered a money bill if, in the opinion of the Speaker, it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following subjects, namely, the imposition, repeal, remission, alteration, or regulation of taxation; charges on the consolidated fund or the provision of money by parliament; supply; the appropriation, control, or regulation of public money; the raising or guarantee of any loan or the repayment thereof: or matters incidental to those subjects or any of them.
So that the definition thus supplied by the resolution of the British House of Commons applies, I submit, to the bill now before the House and further establishes the sole jurisdiction of this House in the matter, and that, Mt. Chairman, I further submit, is an answer to the contention that the sole authority of this House is 'limited to what are called Supply bills.
Does the minister say the Senate has no right to reject the bill?
No, I did not say that..
What does the hon. minister mean by 'sole jurisdiction" if the right of rejection rests with anybody?

To initiate measures for the expenditure of money. Any time this House has accepted an amendment to a money bill, it has always been done under a. protest in the name of the Finance Minister of the day. When my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was Minister of Finance, he did the same thing.
In the last two years we have had no such thing.

We have had a great many of those cases'. My hon. friend referred to opinions given by Messrs. Lafleur and Geof-frion regarding the powers of the Senate in relation to such matters as the one we are discussing. He also very fairly stated that there was another opinion given at the same time by an equally eminent gentleman, Mr. John S. Ewart. It occurs to me that Mr. Ewart's opinion is so much in point that the House would like to hear it, inasmuch as while Mr. Ewart was consulted by the Senate at the same time as Messrs. Geoffrion and Lafleur, he differs entirely from these two gentlemen who are both, as the House knows, very eminent legal authorities but who can scarcely be said to be such close students of constitutional affairs as is Mr. Ewart. Mr. Ewart's opinion is contained in these paragraphs :
From the very earliest time, the colonial assemblies have successfully contended for the same privilege with reference to financial bills as that enjoyed by the British House of Commons. The oases in which contention arose are very numerous, but I do not know of any in which the quarrel between the two Houses has resulted in substantial victory for the Council-as, in the earlier constitutions, the second chamber was styled.
A glance at the histories, furnishes me with two instances which may be taken as containing typical assertion of the privilege of the assemblies. The first, of these is noted in Dickerson's American Colonial Government, 1696-1765: The author says (page 160 that, in the time of Governor Cornbury, of New York:-
"The Council sought to amend the revenue bill so as to remove this objection, but it was met by the point blank assertion that the Assembly would permit no amendment of money bills."
The second instance I take from Dr. Kingsford's book, the History of Canada, volume 9, page 217. On that occasion (181S) the Council and Assembly were brought into sharp conflict with the result, as the author says, that:-
"The Council did not conceive an amendment to the money bill as a breach of privilege; but as it was so asserted, the Council would hereafter forebear from all amendment and simply reject any bill submitted to it, should occasion suggest."
Mr. Ewart concludes:
There can be no doubt that the difference between the British House of Lords and the Canadian Senate referred to in the memorandum are of substantial character, but, after all, the two Houses, with reference to the subject under consideration occupy the same position. For the members of neither House are elected by the people, and the privilege of the Assembly with regard to money bills has always been based upon the fact that the House was composed of [DOT]populariy elected members.
So, I sum up in conclusion that the government in this case has followed the practice that has always been followed in this House; that it has taken the first step by placing the motion that is in your hands be-

Home Bank

fore the House; that that is directly in accordance with parliamentary procedure and practice; that the other steps to which I have alluded will follow automatically, almost as a matter of course if that motion be adopted, and that the conference referred to must take place before it can be known what measure of relief the Home Bank depositors can receive; and finally, that the position taken by the government is! fortified by all the recognized parliamentary authorities.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure it would be presumption on my part to attempt to express an opinion upon the constitutionality of the action taken by the Senate in amending the bill or in creating a new bill in regard to the Home Bank depositors. The House has listened with attention to the remarks made by the Postmaster General, (Mr. Murphy), defining exactly what steps have to be taken in connection with further action that may be undertaken in regard to this matter. I rose only to express this hope that, no matter what takes place, after all the proceedings that have been outlined have been gone on with, should there be any difficulty in getting this bill in its original form or in a form in which this House would accept it without derogating in any way from its dignity, the Home Bank depositors shall not be disappointed. It seems to me that, after what has taken place, it would be not only unjust, but almost cruel, that the thing should fall down now because there is a dispute between the two Houses. Parliament has within its power the means to see to it that what has been promised shall be carried through, and I hope the government will see its way clear before the close of this session, to ensure that, no matter what takes place, the Home Bank depositors shall not be disappointed in the promises that have been made to them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel indebted myself and I think all of us do to the Postmaster General for his calm and scholarly treatment of the government's position. It was some such statement as that which I asked for from the administration when this resolution was suddenly moved at half past five o'clock this afternoon. A resolution some three pages in length involving six by no means brief pronouncements of constitutional doctrine was moved without any notice by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), and the government wanted it to go to a vote without any statement from themselves, any pronouncement of any kind or any ex-

position of the grounds on which the resolution rested. When I asked for it, I was told in a word: Here is this flung at you >'n a second; now get up and vote on it, or if you are not ready to vote, get up and discuss it. This was the consideration which the government felt that the rest of the House were entitled to.
The Senate has amended an important measure of the administration and I admit that the amendments are substantial. I am not criticising the amendments in the main. As the House will recall, when the government's bill was before this chamber, I urged that the principle which appeared to underlie it, if indeed any did, was that of compensation based upon either moral or legal responsibility. I urged that moral responsibility as against a government was equally binding with legal responsibility, but that in my view neither of those existed, and consequently that the principle followed in the bill could not be upheld as a matter of right. I urged, though, that in view of the widespread loss and suffering caused by this financial collapse, a measure of relief dictated by compassion would receive at the hands of this House, in my judgment, a hospitable welcome. Some such view appears to have been taken of the whole transaction by the upper house. It is not within our power to comment upon anything which took place there, to quote any speeches, or in any way to criticize. But it is within my power to call attention to this fact, that the Senate in this matter was unanimous, that the action taken passed with the support of all members of that body.
The bill comes to parliament thus amended, and the government takes the ground that this being a money bill-and I am not disputing that it is a money bill-it is not subject to amendment in any way at all, and that the upper house cannot lay unholy hands upon it; that it must either accept or reject it. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) has shown how utterly inconsistent this is with the reason alleged by the administration for placing this vote in a separate bill in the first place. It was in order that the Senate might enjoy full rights of discussion; that the matter might come before the upper house as before this. These reasons do not amount to very much if the Senate has no power save that of rejection. The whole groundwork collapses; it is smashed by the conduct of the government now.
Now, to the authorities cited by the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) I do not take any exception. Nobody disputes that in this parliament all money bills must originate in

Home Bank
the Commons. The Postmaster General upon my question went a little further but he refused to go beyond this sentence, that not only must the origination be here but the direction as well. I do not know to what that direction has reference.
The money.
That is to say, the destination of it.
Yes.

In other words, this
House alone can decide the destination of it. If I apprehend the Postmaster General's position aright it is this, that the origination of a money bill must be in this House; and with that I agree. And the destination of the money must also be determined here; and therefore the Senate in this particular can make no amendments. The Senate cannot change the destination of the money; that is the contention. Have I correctly stated the hon. member's position?
The distribution of it.

That is implied in its
destination. The Postmaster General, then, in his statement does not deny to the upper house every power of amendment. I thought that was his position and I am pleased to find that I am correct. But he does deny to the Senate any power of amendment which affects the distribution of the money itself. Well, if such is the position of the hon. gentlemen I am afraid he will have to vote against this motion of his government, because the government in its six resolutions challenges not only the right of the Senate to put its finger upon the bill and alter in the least the destination of the money, but it challenges the right of the Senate to alter even the wording of the bill. It challenges the Senate to alter the bill in any regard whatever. It recites in its first paragraph the fact that the Senate has altered the preamble.
That is not quite correct; the Senate has inserted a preamble where there was none before.

That is right; it has inserted a preamble. The first paragraph of the Senate bill recites the fact that a petition has been presented to the government and the further fact that there is no moral responsibility; and it defines the principle of the bill to be the principle of relief. And the government's resolution declares that because the Senate has done these things this House should vote that the Senate is wrong. Now, the House will take more than a moment to observe 304*
that not one of these things affects the destination of the money; not one of them diverts a dollar or a copper; not one of them in any way at all alters the distribution of the money, according to the Postmaster General's exposition of the law, which I am not disputing. The government therefore has no right to ask the House to pronounce in favour of resolution No. 1.
Now I pass to another of these resolutions, No. 3. But before I do so let me make a general reference to the authorities quoted by the Postmaster General; and as I do so I may be permitted to emphasize that I am in complete accord with him as to the jurisdiction of this House and this House alone to originate money bills and to name the destination. Nor will I fall away from the assertion of power contained in rule 78. But let us take up the history of this matter. This house of parliament, is not necessarily in the position of the houses referred to in Redlich, as quoted by the hon. gentleman. It may be and it may not be. It is not necessarily in the position of the British House. It may or it may not be. Certainly it is true that neither our Senate nor the Senate of Australia has the powers of the British House of Commons; but it at least is subject to very serious dispute whether the whole power rests in this Commons or iD the British House of Commons. Very eminen authorities have differed on this point and I do not feel myself competent to express an opinion upon it. Certainly the reasoning of Messrs. Geoffrion and Lafleur seems more convincing than the reasoning of Mr. Ewart. Mr. Ewart has left out of account the difference in Canada's status from the fact that it if established by the British North America Act and that alone. The British North America Act is our charter and upon that rock rests not only the Commons but the Senate as well. And here in this Dominion, in view of the fact that confederation is a compact which all the provinces came into, the Senate may quite naturally exercise, indeed was given, powers beyond the powers exercised by the Lords of England, because the Senate was looked upon as destined to be the repository of minority rights. The dictum of the Postmaster General is certainly by no means accepted as true, that if you can establish some sole jurisdiction in the Commons of England it follows that such jurisdiction is in the Commons of Canada. I would ask the hon. gentleman to read the opinion which Mr. Geoffrion and Mr. Lafleur expressed in this regard, and I fancy they will at least agree with me that there is room for grave doubt and argument on this point. The British North America Act refers to the matter
Home Bank

in two clauses and two clauses alone. In section 53 quoted in the resolution it is provided:
Bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue, or for imposing any tax or* impost, shall originate m the House of Commons.
Therefore on this the Postmaster General is right; no one can. dispute that. And section 54 reads:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, rOF cf any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by message of the Governor General in the session in which such wcte, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
These are the clauses in the British North America Act relating to this question and to them we must appeal. I think it follows from the first, not only that the origination must be here but that, inasmuch as the destiny of the .money is itself one of the inherent circumstances of the origination, the Senate may not change the destiny. That would be originating a new vote. The Postmaster General is therefore well advised in restricting his final statement of the law in the manner he has stated iit. No on.e could go any further, and so I state again that this resolution cannot be supported on the statement of law to which the Postmaster General confines himself and rightly confines himself. 'Let us look at clause 3, which is a most remarkable one.
Because clause (a) added to the bill provides for the appointment of a commissioner and the organization of a lengthy and costly procedure, thereby entailing a large expenditure which the Senate has no right to make a charge upon the public revenues, and which could only be authorized if it had first been recommended by the Governor General in Council and voted by the House of Commons, under sections 53 and 54 of the British North America Act.
This is indeed remarkable. But what does clause (a) declare? Clause (a) of the Senate bill simply provides that the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada shall, on such evidence as seems to him sufficient, dispose of this money, first, to all who have deposits of $500 or under, and secondly, to such others as the necessities of relief demand that they should receive something.
Does the hon. member think that an investigation 'by an Exchequer court judge into 47,000 cases will entail no expenditure of money?

Forty-seven thousand
cases? After the five hundred dollar cases there are only a few to be dealt with. There is nothing whatever in the act that would prevent the Exchequer court judge, sitting right in his office here in Ottawa, having everyone come to him and testify, or receiving by affidavit all the evidence he would need

to act upon. I do not say that that is what he -would do; he would probably go around -there would likely be expense; that is quite true; but you cannot assume it, and you must be forced to assume it before this clause 3 can stand. In a word, there is nothing in the bill itself which makes absolutely compulsory the expenditure of a single dollar.

My right hon. friend will
observe that the president of the Exchequer court is to act personally, and not as a judge of that court.

Very good; that does
not affect my point.
As to expense?

He cannot under the
law get any money.

What about additional
expense?

There is nothing in this
about additional expense.

How can he do the work
otherwise?

I am not arguing that
he will not do it, but there must be something in the law which compels him to do it before this objection can lie. There is nothing whatever in the statute.
Is it not a necessary incident?
No; he can do the whole thing for charity.

My right hon. friend's
other argument was much stronger than the last.
The other argument was impregnable, and this is impregnable too. If the hon. gentleman feels I am wrong in this, there are precedents he can follow.

I should not like to say
my right hon. friend is wrong, but he certainly is not right.

Well, in my eventful
life I have always been content with that degree of rectitude which keeps me always not wrong. I can refer my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) to authorities on this very point, authorities for whom he has the highest regard himself, who agree with every word I say. The bill must necessarily impose a charge before this objection can lie.

Now, what are these other exceptions th$t have struck the conscience of the government so badly? It says:
Because it is provided by clause 7 of the said bill as passed by the House of Commons that "the Governor in Council may raise by way of loan, temporary or otherwise, upon such form of security and upon such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve, such sum or sums of money as are required for the purpose of making the payment authorized by this act, and any sum so raised shall form part of the consolidated revenue fund," and the raising of anj' loan as a charge upon the consolidated revenue fund is the undoubted and sole privilege of the Commons.
Well, will hon. gentlemen believe that this clause to which the government takes such violent objections is in its own bill untouched, unchallenged in any particular? The Senate has not dotted an I or crossed a T. Apparently it is the opinion of the government that before the Senate could come with virtuous hands, it should have deleted the government's own clause! Can the government ask the House to vote for a resolution such as this? How scrupulous, how virtuous it has become all of a sudden! Hon. gentlemen will remember bill after bill-money bills in exactly the same sense that this is a money bill-altered by the Senate, substantially altered in vital clauses, but with never a word of protest, no resolution thrust upon the House without a second's notice, no resolution at all; in a word, the government accepted those alterations. Strange indeed that when we come to the Home Bank measure it should be selected as the ground upon which a great constitutional battle is going to be fought before the government will venture another step in the path of relief of the depositors.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming
into the chamber this evening there has been handed to me a letter which in itself is of considerable importance as indicating the point of view which those most interested in this measure are likely to take. It is also of special value as illustrating wherein the course which the government is now proposing, of conferring with the Senate on this matter, is the course which the public generally, and more particularly those who are especially interested in the enactment of some measure of relief, will expect the government to take. It also, I think, serves to illustrate wherein the government from the outset has adopted the correct procedure in dealing with this matter. The letter bears the letterhead of the president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. It is date! Ottawa, June 23, 1923, and is signed by Tom Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Congress
of Canada, L. L. Peltier, legislative, representative of the Order of Railway Conductors, Byron Baker, legislative representative of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, W. L. Best, legislative representative of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Engineers and T. J. Coughlin, legislative representative of the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen. The letter is addressed to myself, and is as follows:
Dear Sir,-
We, the undersigned, desire to bring to your notice the dissatisfaction with which the Senate bill dealing with the affairs of the Home Bank has been received by the members of the organizations which we represent. By its amendments, the Senate has completely changed the purpose and amount of relief to be granted to depositors, as contained in Bill No. 182 passed by the House of Commons, and which measure met with general approval.
Under the bill, as now amended, the preamble is so a'tered as to make any payment an act of charity on the part of the government rather than an act of justice to those who were misled into leaving their deposits in the Heme Bank, through their belief in the efficiency of the protection offered by government supervision of chartered banks.
Further, the need of a person for relief is arbitrarily fixed by the amount of the deposit in the setting of $500 as the sum on which 35 per cent of such deposit shall be paid merely upon application. Others in actual need will find it necessary, if the Senate bill is accepted, to disclose all of their private affairs in order to obtain simple justice and finding it necessary to engage legal aid will, we fear, in many cases, have very little of their savings in their own hands at the finish.
Then again, municipal councils, fraternal societies, churches and labour unions are debarred from participation even though these deposits actually represent, :n most cases, the mutual investment of people without wealth. Presumably this is also based upon the premise that relief to the depositors is an act of charity.
All of this we respectfully submit is wrong and without entering, at this time, into lengthy arguments in support of this statement, desire to point out that it is corroborated by the findings of the commissioners appointed to investigate this whole matter and on whose report the bill passed by the House of Commons was based.
We. therefore, earnestly urge your government o maintain the principle of equal compensation to all depositors (irrespective of the amount or character of the deposit) and the payment of such compensation as an act of justice and not as an act of charity.
If this is impossible of accomplishment in harmony with the Senate, then we would suggest that the will of the peoples' elected representatives be given effect by placing the sum of $5,450,000 in the supplementary estimates to be distributed in accordance with the terms embodied in Bill No. 182, as passed by the House of Commons on June 10, 1925.
With respect to the suggestion that an amount should be placed in the estimates, may I point out to the House that so far as hon. gentlemen opposite are concerned the depositors of the Home Bank would be in exactly the same position as they will be under this bill as amended by the Senate. The bill in its amended form, as this letter from the president of the Trades and Labour Congress and other labour representatives indicates,
Howe Bank

takes away relief entirely on the ground of moral right, and substitutes relief solely on compassionate grounds, which is the ground being urged by hon. gentlemen opposite. Now, that ground is just as applicable whether the money is paid out under an estimate passed by this House, or paid out under the provisions of a bill which has been approved by both houses of parliament. In each case exactly the same arguments apply. If depositors who are entitled to more than $500 can be paid under the bill as originally introduced by the government, and not under the bill as amended, neither will it be possible to pay them, according to the point of view of hon. gentlemen opposite, from any estimate that may be brought into this House. Were an estimate brought in for the amount of $5,450,000, which is the amount named in the bill, the right hon. leader of the opposition would be obliged, in accordance with the position which he and his party have taken, to move that that estimate be cut down to the amount mentioned in the bill as it now comes t-o us from the Senate. He would be obliged to move that all consideration of municipal councils, fraternal societies, churches, labour unions, and so on, be struck out. He would be obliged to take the position, as I have already indicated, that any persons entitled to more than $500 in the way of relief should not be given that relief.
Try it that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend says, "try it." I am presenting an argument to the House of Commons; I am presenting the reason for the position the government has taken from the outset.

I do not think the Prime
Minister is quite fair to this party. I only speak for myself, but he has no right to couple me with what he has said. Personally I am in favour of relief for the depositors of the Home Bank, and I have so expressed myself on many occasions. If this House wants to be in control of it, let the amount be put in the estimates, and we shall have no trouble with the Senate. I am prepared to support it. I rise to make these few remarks now, because unfortunately I was away on the previous occasion when the vote came on. There are a great many depositors of the Home Bank in my riding-not the riding as it will be under the redistribution, but the riding I at present represent.
Order.

Well, I am only going to be a moment. There are 2,900 of these depositors in my riding, representing deposits in three branches of the bank and covering an aggregate amount, I understand, of over $600,-
000.	Many of these are very needy cases. It is my keen desire to support any proposal for their relief, and if the government sincerely and honestly want to put through a measure of relief, let the bill with the Senate amendments go by the board, bring in an estimate, and put it through the House, and so far as I am concerned I will vote for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I can only
say it is unfortunate that my hon. friend (Mr. Boys) was not here to differ from those of his own party when the matter was discussed before. The position taken by the right hon. leader of the opposition to-night in this debate-

The right hon. gentleman might be a little fairer. I stated distinctly when I spoke on this measure before that I favoured relief on the basis of compensation and that in that I was sorry I could not represent the party as a party, that I spoke for myself. I made that very plain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
A good many
of my hon. friends opposite spoke at the same time, including the hon. member for West York, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) who took precisely the same line that my right hon. friend took at the time and which he has taken again to-night. That is the position taken by his friends in the other House.
Many of our members supported the bill.

And by the right hen.
gentleman's friends in the other House, too.

speechtext: Order, please. My right hon. friend has had his opportunity to speak.
Well, be correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I want to repeat that the government in this matter acted in accordance, first of all, with the finding of the royal commission; in the second place, it, acted in accordance with the recommendation of the Banking and Commerce committee, and in the third place it acted in accordance with the unanimous report of this House of Commons, which hon. gentlemen opposite, along with other hon. members of this House approved and which declared that there was a moral claim, a claim in equity,

Home Bank
in respect to those who had lost their deposits as the result of the Home Bank disaster. It was solely on that basis that the bill was brought in. I contend that if a bill had been brought in on any other basis hon. gentlemen opposite would have had ample ground to criticize the administration for having appointed a commission, for having referred the commission's report to a committee of the House, for having taken a vote of the House on the report of the committee, with the result that it was endorsed by the House, and having then failed to act on this authority, which was constitutional in every particular.

Will the right
hon. gentleman allow me a question? Does the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) admit that there was a moral claim?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, the Acting Minister of Finance was in his seat, I think, at the time the resolution passed this House, and voted for it. At any rate, the government speaks as one; the position of the government is that there is a moral claim and a bill has been brought in on that basis.
I venture to say that the Acting Minister of Finance does take the same position; so far as I am aware, he has never differed in any particular from any of his colleagues on this matter. Certainly it would be extraordinary if the government brought in a bill, through one of its members, for which the government as a whole was not prepared to take the full responsibility.
It would not be extraordinary for this government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not an extraordinary remark from my hon. friend. With regard to the action which the House is called upon to take at the moment, may I say that all the House is being asked by the motion is to express either its concurrence or its non-concurrence in the amendments which the Senate has proposed to the bill. The course which the government has taken in that regard, as has been explained two or three times to-day, is the proper constitutional course of proceeding. On two or three occasions this session bills have come to this House from the Senate, amended in a manner not satisfactory to the House. In such cases the minister in charge has outlined in the form of a written statement the reasons why the amendments as presented were not satisfactory to the government. Hon. gentlemen opposite will recall that only a few evenings ago a measure of that character relating to some phase of agriculture came to this House.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) was not in his seat at that time, and in order that time might be saved, that this House might discover without delay whether or not the Senate was prepared to alter its decision in virtue of the reasons advanced, I read to the House myself the reasons which the Minister of Agriculture had outlined in the statement to be presented to their honours of the Senate. These reasons went to the Senate without discussion, the members of the Senate examined them and accepted the advice or suggestions of the Commons, so that the further step of a conference was not necessary. The government in this matter has proceeded in precisely the same way. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition has no reason to say that there was any discourtesy to him or to any member of the House when the Acting Minister of Finance presented a carefully drafted statement intended for their honours in the Senate, and which set out fully the reasons why the government could not concur in the amendments which were made. It is true that the Acting Minister of Finance did not himself read the reasons; he left it to his honour the Speaker to read them. But as I interpreted his action at the time, it was simply to save the time that would be involved in reading the reasons over twice in succession. That was the sole reason why the Acting Minister of Finance did not read them himself, but the procedure in every particular is precisely that which is adopted when the Commons is unable to agree to amendments proposed by the Senate. As I have said, the purpose of the government in sending these reasons to the other chamber is that members of that House may have an opportunity to consider carefully the point of view of the Commons in this matter. Having had that opportunity the Senate will intimate to us what their action is likely to be. My hope would be that the Senate would find it possible to make a change in the amendments which they have proposed. Some they may not wish to change; others they may find good reason to change. At any rate, it is not for this House to say what the further step shall be until we receive word back from the Senate as to whether they agree with our reasons here.
Can the Prime Minister give us any idea when we shall likely have word back from the Senate in regard to this matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, the
Senate is moving with a good deal of rapidity these days. Hon. members of the Senate
Home Bank

seem to be getting through a greal deal of work, and I have every reason to believe they will wish to meet the desires of all concerned by acting in this matter promptly. I see no reason why we should not get back word from the Senate within a very few hours after they have had had an opportunity of studying this matter.
Let me make one thing perfectly plain: There is no desire on the part of the government in any way to have this matter shelved. Let me make it clear that the government intends to stay here and see that as much as possible is secured to the Home Bank depositors as it is possible to obtain in a constitutional way, and if the Senate is slow in	returning an answer, we
will be here awaiting that answer until it comes. There is no effort on the part of the administration to have this matter delayed. The references which have been made to a constitutional conference, are all beside the mark. It is important the government should place its position clearly on record. It may well be that the conference that will take place between members of this House and members of the Senate, should such a conference be held in further discussion of the reasons alleged here for not accepting the amendments, will not enter into a full discussion of the constitutional relations of the two Houses, but it may nevertheless be sufficient to decide what is the answer with respect to this measure. It is important, however, that the government's position should be clearly stated and of record for all time in the future.

Assuming the motion carries
and a conference results with representatives of the Senate, which conference proves abortive, will the Prime Minister favour the inclusion in further supplementary estimates of the item of $5,400,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is trying to rush matters unduly. This present motion is not for a conference. It is for the purpose of asking their honours of the Senate to consider the reasoned arguments of this House as to why the amendments which they have proposed should not be inserted in the bill. I submit it would be a discourtesy to the Senate, to say nothing else, for this House to assume for one moment that their honours of the Senate will not accept this reasoned statement in the spirit in which it is being sent to them. At any rate, I do not propose to pass judgment on the Senate's attitude in this matter until the proper time comes for so doing.

I asked the Prime Minister
to indicate his own view, if he would.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am indicating the view of the government with regard to this matter and that, I think, should be sufficient, for my hon. friend.
I just wished to make one further reference which I unfortunately omitted the other day to make. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Dray,ton) intimated that the leader of the government in the Senate, so I understood him to say, accepted the Senate's point of view in regard to this matter.
He moved the third reading.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
H there is any impression of that kind, I would ask hon.
members to refer themselves to the debates in the Senate, which I am precluded from referring to here, and they will find that the leader of the government in the Senate distinctly stated-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend was particularly careful not to correct hiis colleague when he reflected on the leader of the government in the Senate. I am quite prepared to leave to the House 'his omission to correct his colleague for the reflection he made on the leader of the government in the Senate, and the present attitude of the right hon. gentleman in not permitting me to state the position of the government accurately, as it should be stated.

Might I be permitted to say a word before the debate closes? I have listened to it with very deep interest, and I have come to the conclusion that there is not a very great difference of opinion between the view taken by the government in regard to this matter and the view which is taken on this side of the House. The trouble, I think, has arisen largely from the manner in which the government has brought the .matter before the House. Certainly an important question such as the present one should not be brought in without a moment's notice, and with an. insistence upon the part of tine Acting {Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that the matter must go on without time for consideration or re-

Home Bank
flection, that we .must either accept or reject the motion as it is presented to us.
One has only to read this resolution to conclude that it is a serious declaration of constitutional right on the part of this House by the government of the day, and I think I am quite within the mark when I say that there are questions raised in this resolution which call for the most careful consideration by the ablest 'lawyers in the House before a satisfactory conclusion could be reached as to the propriety of the resolution.
10 p.m. The .objection taken by my right hon. leader to the resolution is that it goes too far as a declaration of constitutional right.
There are three specific allegations in this resolution to which my right hon. leader takes exception, and I think he is on solid ground in the exception which he takes. On the real issue before .us there seems to be no difference of opinion. The real question is, has the Senate power either to originate or amend a money bill of this House by changing the destiny of the appropriation? I think it is clear beyond question that the Senate has not that power. So we are agreed on the main point. Therefore, why hamper the resolution by dragging in three very doubtful assertions of right?
First, it is said that the Senate has no power to amend the preamble or, to insert a preamble. I do not know upon what ground that claim is asserted. There is nothing in section 53 of the British North America Act bo say the Senate has no such power. There is nothing in rule 78 of this House to say the Senate has no such power, and our whole authority in this matter is derived from section 53 of the British North America Act and rule 78 of this House. That is the first objection: We are asserting a right, and a very doubtful right, to say the least.

But the Senate by adding a preamble to the bill may include a new principle altogether.
.Mr. GUTHRIE: There may be something in that argument, but the preamble of the billl is not the enacting clause of the bill. It may be an explanatory clause of the bill, I agree, but there .is nothing in the rules of this House and nothing in the British North America Act to say the Senate may not amend the preamble of a bill. It may not change the destination of a grant, nor can it originate the grant.
'Mr. VIEN: Yet it did in this bill.
In so far as it did, I say its action is beyond its power, and my right hon. leader agrees with me in that.

Will my hon. friend allow me to draw his attention to the fact that the resolution.-I have not a copy of it before me and I am speaking from recollection- does not take exception to the insertion of the preamble, but rather to what the preamble recites, purporting to speak both on behalf of the government and on behalf of the House of Commons.

It certainly raises the
question whether the Senate is right in doing what it has done. I think it is a point which may well be argued in favour of the Senate, but it is unnecessary, in order to obtain our purpose, to make any assertion of that right at the present time.
In the second place, it is said that because the Senate has directed a commission to enquire-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Might I
ask my hon. friend a question on a point as to which I am not quite clear? He argues that the Senate cannot affect the destiny of a money vote. I agree that that is a
rejection of part of the vote of this House, and the Senate has gone beyond its power in so doing.
On the second point, my right hon. leader says that the provision in the Senate's amendment for the payment of a commission to distribute the money is not necessarily a charge upon the exchequer of this country, and does not create a tax or impost. In that I think he is technically right. Then why seek to assert, as this resolution does, that the Senate has done wrong in that? I want to make myself clear on that. There is never a public bill brought into this House that does not entail some expense in carrying it out. During my time in the. House again and again, it has been said by Mr. Speaker that where the bill is not one to impose a tax, or create a loan, or expend money, the mere consequential expenditure in the administration of the bill does not necessitate its going before His Excellency for consent before being introduced to this House. This at most could be but a consequential expense. It is not a tax or impost. Why assert it as a right?
Home Bank

Why the unnecessary assertion of it in this resolution? The first objection is that the resolution says that section 7 of the Senate bill has authorized something which it has no right to authorize; but section 7 of the Senate bill and section 6 of the House of Commons bill are identical, word for word. The Senate cannot have transgressed its right in that respect. My suggestion is that these three unnecessary or improper assertions of right should be withdrawn from the resolution. We are agreed on the main point; we agree that the Senate has gone beyond its power in regard to the amendment of a money bill. On the vital question there is no dispute. Why not let our representation be unanimous and withdraw

Is my hon. friend speaking
for all the members on his side of the House?

No, I cannot speak for
anyone except myself. I do not think in the riding which I have the honour to represent there is a single depositor or slockholder in the Home Bank, but I am heartily in favour of the bill and want to see it passed. I was not here when it was brought into the House originally, but I desire that the bill as passed in this House become law, and why not let us agree on the method of procedure by dropping what is not essential and is doubtful?
Will my hon. friend's leader agree to what he says? He had better canvass his own leader before canvassing us.

If the three matters raised by my right hon. friend were deleted from the motion, I think he would accept the balance, as he stated in his speech a few minutes ago, and that is the course which I ask the government to pursue.

The question I
asked the Prime Minister was based on statements which I found in Hansard of June 8, at pave 3961, as follows:
Sir Henry Drayton: No, the wealthy man and the
poor man.
Mr. Robb: The wealthy man and the poor man- if it is a moral claim, how are we going to differentiate between those two?
Mr. Meighen: Does the minister himself think there is a moral claim against the country?
Mr. Robb: I am dealing now with the report of the Banking and Commerce committee, which was unanimously concurred in by this House.
Mr. Meighen: We will discuss that later. But will the minister answer me directly: does he himself consider there is a moral claim against this country?
Mr. Robb: I am not debating that question. I was a member of the Banking and Commerce committee. In this country majorities are supposed to rule. We are carrying out in this respect the views of parliament.

I would point out that this export of $142,000,000 compares favourably with the export of any other class of goods from this country. For example, a few minutes ago I looked up the exports of wheat, which perhaps is the largest individual export from Canada, and I find that in 1924 we shipped out $267,000,000 worth of this commodity, or a little over $100,000,000 more than we did of pulp and paper. This past year however the exports of wheat had fallen to $235,000,000. I mention these figures merely for the purpose of indicating the importance of this immense industry, which calls for as much attention a3 any other line of endeavour in Canada. And I cattnot forget that I come from a section

Indeed, so extensive is its area that its width from east to west is nearly equal to the width of any two of the prairie provinces together Unfortunately however it forms a large gap between the east and the west and this is a handicap in many directions of our national life. One of our railway difficulties in Canada is due to this very fact that we have 700 miles of territory in width, covering some three and a half million square miles in area, with a population of only 150,000 or so. This forms a very serious gap between east ffnd west not only to the disadvantage of the railways but to the disadvantage of our national life as well. In that northern section of Ontario the pulp and paper industry to-day is probably the most important of our activities. The industry supplies the railways of that section of the country with a large proportion of their business. I think, too, of the great development of our hydro-electric energy in northern Ontario which is used to a considerable extent by the pulp and paper industry. The pulp and paper industry being of so much importance to that part of the country, which is still more or less undeveloped, I feel it my duty, in loyalty to that section of northern Ontario, to support this proposition.
I should like to point out a few other reasons which I think are worthy of consideration. In the next parliament, if I were handling the affairs of the country, and if I had put into force a treaty such as this with the Commonwealth of Australia, it would be my endeavour to protect the farmers of Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and the Maritime provinces by raising the tariffs against the United States and all other countries, but leaving the Australian treaty in force. By doing that I would accomplish two things, I would not only bring about a species of assistance to the farmers mentioned by putting out the competition of foreign countries, but I would enhance to Australia the value of her treaty with us. My hon. friend will remember that two years ago, I think it was the session of 1923, the matter of Australian trade treaty was before parliament for consideration. The explanation of that is this:	Our trade witlh Australia is
very many times greater than Australia's trade with Canada. The government of Australia, in seeking to enter into an agreement with Canada, was immediately confronted with that large favourable balance
of trade on Canada's side, and the Australian government made it clear to our government that unless some concession was given with respect to some commodities of which Australia had exportable quantities it would be useless to attempt any kind of reciprocal arrangement. That is one factor to take into account in considering the possible effect of a duty on raisins against other countries and the removal of the duty as against Australia and other countries of the British Empire. To-day under the British preference there is. a duty of a half cent on raisins; that will be removed under this agreement, and so far as British countries to which we give a preference are concerned raisins will come in free. They will come in free, therefore, not only from Australia but from many parts of the British Empire. Australia is not the only part of the British Empire that produces raisins. South Africa, I understand, produces raisins and currants in quantities. At the Imperial Economic Conference which was attended by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and myself two years ago in London, the then Prime Minister of South Africa, Mr. Smuts, gave us to understand that the balance of trade as between Canada and South Africa was so much in favour of Canada that unless Canada would make concessions to South Africa in respect to some commodities, the South African government w'ould be obliged to change its fiscal relations toward this Dominion. He spoke particularly at that time of South Africa's ability to send currants and raisins to this country if they got a favourable opportunity.

I am telling my hon. friend what was represented to the Minister of Railways and myself, when we were at the Imperial Economic Conference, by the then Prime Minister of South Africa, which representations I think have been confirmed by' further correspondence which has taken place between the Minister of Finance and the government ar South Africa. More than that, it is hardly probable that the country to the south is going to sacrifice this market which is right at its door. Surely there is something to be said for seeking to develop trade between the different parts of the empire. For twenty years this country has been seeking to make an arrangement with Australia. May I draw attention to this further circumstance? In dealing with Australia it is not as though we were negotiating with our neighbour immediately to our south, where competition is likely to make itself instantly and effectively felt. We are dealing with a country that is seven thousand miles from Vancouver by sea, a trip on a fast vessel of some three weeks, and a journey of some six weeks by the ordinary ships carrying the commodities that are likely to enter into competition. equator, which means that foodstuffs and the

I stress these points because I feel, and the government feels very strongly that this is an opportunity to begin a trade between a sister Dominion and our own nation which will grow and expand as the years go by. There is an old saying that trade begets trade, and 305
