My hon. friend made, fo, a beginner, a very good free trade speech. I am not surprised, because I think it is as certain as anything can be that the section of the Dominion from which he comes ie going to change its views in respect of fiscal protection. You cannot have a great city like Vancouver situated on the Pacific ocean, where the great trade development of this century will take place, without the natural sentiment growing there in favour of extending its trade to the ends of the earth.
When we come to a consideration of the treaty, I confess that I do not magnify it to the position of importance that some hon. members have given it. The total volume of our trade with Australia last year, as we were informed this evening by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) approximates some $14,000,000 or $15,000,000. Taken with the total volume of Canadian trade for the past year, it is comparatively insignificant. The government, however, are to be commended for endeavouring to improve the interchange of goods with this distant continent of Australia. Personally, I would be much more pleased if the government endeavoured to direct some energy to improving our trade relations with our great neighbour to the south. Considerably more than one-half of Canadian trade is done with the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would submit that measures of this kind will help to bring about the very thing at which my hon. friend is aiming. When our neighbours to the south find that unless they trade with us, we are going to do more of our trade with othel parts of the world, they will come to time much more quickly than they otherwise would.
Australian Treaty

I believe the Prime Minister is right. I would not quarrel with his assertion; but while we are endeavouring to promote trade with Australia, Latvia, Poland, France and Italy, we have done practically nothing-and we might be able to .do something if we tried-towards creating a better feeling with the United States in trade matters. We should have several good trade commissioners in the United States. We should have at Washington a good practical man who would tell United States senators and congressmen that Canada is a country worth while trading with. I believe in that respect this country could do a great deal to aid in promoting better trade relations with the United States, and no ^natter where we trade to the ends of the earth, I venture to predict that for decades to come the larger volume of Canadian trade, from the very nature of our geopraphical relations, will be done with the United States.
When we come to the treaty itself, there are one or two things that are open to criticism. I support the criticism expressed by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) and one or two others in this section of the House in voicing my regret that it was necessary to increase the duty on raisins and currants from the United States in order to get this arrangement. But notwithstanding that, I find, on examination of the treaty, that it tends to pTomote trade between Australia and Canada by reducing the barriers that have hitherto existed, and for that reason I am going to support it. I am not even in the most remote way impressed with the arguments advanced this evening by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and some other hon. gentlemen to my right that we are in danger of putting the Canadian farmer out of business by introducing into Canada at these lower rates of duty similar produce from the continent of Australia. If we look at the treaty in that respect, we find that we are proposing to give Australia some preference in duty on eggs. Is that going to put the egg industry in Canada out of business?

I did not suggest that it
would put anything out of business. All I said was that there would be more competition.

I do not think it will put the egg industry in Canada out of business. In fact, I believe there are cases where this may be of decided advantage to Canada. It

may stimulate our own hens to lay better eggs. The little province of Prince Edward Island is one of the great egg-producing sections of Canada.

The Acting Minister of
Finance suggested that if this treaty goes into effect, our breakfast table will be cheaper. That would refer to butter, eggs and so on.

If it makes the breakfast
table cheaper, that is not a bad thing for many Canadians.

Not so good for the hon.
member's constituency.

Prince Edward Island
produces a vast quantity of eggs. At certain seasons of the year the people of Vancouver may want to get eggs that are fairly fresh. I understand at the present time they are importing them on certain occasions from China, but they may prefer to get them from Australia a little cheaper than would be possible say, from Prince Edward Island.

Does my hon. friend not
think it would be better to use good Canadian eggs than either Australian or Chinese eggs?

Yes, and notwithstanding
this treaty, that is -what is going to happen, because Australian eggs will not compete with good Canadian eggs. We export about 150,000,000 pounds of cheese a year. Is anyone going to argue that the little cheese we may bring in from Australia will damage the cheese industry of this country? The same may be said all down the line. I notice in the treaty there is a reduction on sugar coming into Canada I may say, in passing, that in a conversation I had with Dr. Page, treasurer of the Commonwealth government, when he was here a few months ago, he intimated the expectation of the Australian government that there was a great future for the sugar industry in that continent. If this proves true, our consumers in Canada who use sugar are going to get some benefit, and that in any case will be some compensation for the slightly additional price we have to pay for raisins and currants, if indeed we have to pray any more for these commodities. Then further, on the other side of the bargain, we are getting entry into the Australian market for certain important classes of manufactured goods from Canada. I have frequently before criticized the Canadian manufacturers because of their inability to get into the markets of the world and sell their goods there. If I can do anything to assist the Canadian manufacturer to get markets outside I am willing to do it. In fact, the greatest need of

Australian Treaty
Canada to-day is markets for the commodities she produces, and anything that will increase the opportunity of securing those markets,
I care not whether they be for the products of forest or farm, of mine or factory, is a good thing for Canada as a whole. I do not know that the treaty will produce the great results some of my hon. friends anticipate but I do think that it is a step in the right direction. It is a step whereby the barriers of trade between these two dominions are reduced, and for that reason in my judgment, and to the extent that it does that, it is a good thing, and I shall support it.

I want to say just a few
words with regard to the matter of raisins. Some time ago there was an interesting article in the London Economist with reference to this suggested treaty with Australia and it referred to the subject of raisins. I shall for a few minutes make a comparison between Australian and Californian raisins. The Australian raisins will be up against certain expenses which the Californian product will not be charged with. There will be in the first place a loading charge and secondly, rail freight, and there will be also ocean freight and insurance. The Acting Minister of Finance may say that the California men will be up against the first two charges as well. That may be so, but the Australian will still have to bear the extra ocean charge and insurance. The next point is rather an important one. I understand that Australia does not seed any of its raisins while the raisins from California are seedless. This will make a considerable difference to the buyers. The California raisins are also ready I understand in October and November and they get here in time for the winter trade when people are going in more for cakes and pies and when they use the greatest supply of raisins. On . the other hand, the Australian raisins are ripe in March and April and they will not get here until about June when the fresh fruits are coming in. This would mean that a great deal of the crop would have to go into storage. The article in question goes on to say that the common way of storing raisins is to put them in oil, and this gives them a not very palatable taste to a number of people. If these are facts I should be glad if the acting minister would either verify or deny them. At any rate they would make a great deal of difference to the success or otherwise of the arrangement with Australia so far as raisins are concerned. The last point is this. Are the Australians prepared to sell their raisins at a price low enough to make it impossible for the California raisin growers to compete, or
will they, as many or most protected interests do, put up the price of their raisins so high that the California raisin growers will be able to climb over the tariff wall and make as much as they are making to-day?

What has happened to
that 75 per cent clause which worried the minister so much a little while ago?

I have a cablegram which I
have received from the commissioner and which I shall read for the information of my right hon. friend. It is dated from Melbourne, June 18:
Am assured by Minister of Trade and Customs that exactly the same treatment as extended to United Kingdom and other British possessions will be extended to Canada as basis for preference respecting application of labour and material and conditions imports from Canada. I am of opinion conditions are less arbitrary than regulations read.
Ross.

Was it ever suggested
that Canada would be in any different position from England in respect to that clause?
Yes.
Never in the world.
That was our objection to it.

I asked the government
what the objection was and they said that it was passed after the treaty had been made. But there was never any suggestion that it applied peculiarly to Canada.

My hon. friend is right in
that they made some reservation, respecting certain raw materials from the United Kingdom. They explained to us that when Dr. Page was here he said it was not directed against Canada particularly; it was directed against certain imports that were going down to Australia through the British channel of commerce. We replied to Dr. Page, "That will be all right, but why discriminate against *Canada?'' He promised to straighten the matter out but this was not done until Mr. Ross went there.

But it is still 75 per
cent against Canada.
But there is no discrimination.
What was the discrimination before?
I have not that detail here.

The history of this matter is interesting as is the history of the whole treaty, and I may as well say a few words upon it now. The government started, I think, shortly after getting into office on a series of
Australian Treaty

negotiations and perambulations designed to end in a treaty with Australia. At length a treaty or an agreement or whatever else hon. gentlemen may care to call it was entered into about a year ago. This is a phase of the matter which seems to have escaped discussion up to now. Australia and Canada came to an arrangement almost a year ago; apparently the word of Canada was given for the word of Australia. If I am wrong I want to be corrected. The 'Canadian government agreed to submit to their parliament for ratification the terms of an arrangement with that dominion. At all events the Prime Minister of Australia so stated in the Australian parliament, and the terms of that arrangement he submitted to his parliament for approval. The Australian parliament accepted the advice of its government and approved, and all that was wanting then to the consummation of the contract was the approval of the Dominion of Canada through its parliament. Its government had approved. Parliament opened on February 5, reference was made to this, as to other treaties in the Address, as about to be submitted for ratification, but as the session proceeded nothing was introduced. Whereupon repeated inquiries were made as to the reason for the delay. The government gave one reason, and one only-that Australia had passed some clause, not annexed to this arrangement at all, but some general customs law under which goods that were to get the benefit of a preference into Australia must, subject to certain conditions, be manufactured 75 per cent in the country which got the preference. The government said they could not go on with the treaty and ask parliament to ratify it until this was rectified. This general customs law was passed after the arrangement was made. I submitted to the Acting Minister of Finance that Canada was not really affected by that law, that the goods we sold to Australia were 75 per cent manufactured here; but he persisted that this had to be taken care of and he could not go on with the treaty in the meantime. Consequently Canada was in new negotiations with Australia. Now the minister would never suggest to this House, never has suggested since the .treaty came down and the facts are revealed, that this 75 per cent law was the cause of the delay at all. What are the facts? The treaty which the minister had negotiated with Australia, which this government gave its word of honour to Australia it would submit to parliament for ratification, was a wholly different treaty from the one which comes before us now.
The treaty which they submitted to us for ratification appears in the records of the

Australian House. It provided, it is true, for virtually, if not exactly, the same concessions on the part of Australia, concessions to our newsprint manufacturers, to our canned soimon manufacturers, and a certain 2i per cent advantage to certain manufacturers of vehicle parts. Those were in the first treaty as in this. In the first treaty, as in this, agriculture was called upon to pay for those advantages. But agriculture got some compensation. The British preferential tariff against mixed farm products was reduced, and Australia given that reduced tariff. It was reduced substantially. But, on the other hand, the general tariff on these same products was raised, and the Canadian farmer in that respect got a quid pro quo for what he lost. I have before me the details of that treaty, and I do not think I could do better than to give some of them to the House, and I will hand to Hansard the comparative data which gives the present tariff,-British preferential and general ;-the first treaty which the government themselves actually consummated, subject to ratification by parliament; the British preferential and the general tariff there, and as well the British preferential and the general tariff under the present treaty. The columns of this table give it as to the whole twenty classes of articles, mainly farm products. For example, our present tariff on meats, British preferential, is two cents, three cents general. Under the treaty made first this was reduced, British preferential to one cent, but the general tariff was raised to four cents. In the present treaty the preferential tariff which Australia gets is reduced to half a cent; the general tariff is not reduced at all, it is just left where it is to-day. Indeed, right down the line all the Canadian farmer got by way of additional advantage in his home market in lieu of what he had to pay Australia for the newsprint manufacturers and others is wiped completely away-wiped away on meats, wiped away on canned meats, canned poultry and game, extracts of meats, fluid beef, soups and so forth, completly eliminated; on lard the same is done, and on tallow. Take, for example, lard, our present tariff is a cent and a half British preferential, two cents general; the first treaty half a cent British preferential, two and a half cents general. Now it is free to Australia and the two cent general tariff stays Eggs, cheese, beeswax, butter, tomatoes and other vegetables, including corn and baked beans in cans or other airtight packages, and so forth, the present tariff is one cent British preferential, one and a half cents general. The first treaty was to reduce the

Australian Treaty
one cent to three-quarters and give that to Australia, but to add to the general tariff making it one and three-quarter cents. Now, Australian vegetables come in here absolutely free, and the general tariff stays just where it was, a cent and a half. Apples, dried, desiccated or evaporated, ten per cent; pears and some other kinds of fruit, reduced from fifty cents per one hundred pounds to twenty-five cents; raisins and dried currants are similarly treated. Our farmers do not raise raisins and currants-they cannot be raised in Canada, so far as I know. The general tariff is raised on these to three cents. It does no good to the Canadian producer. It probably will do good to Canadian revenue, but I am discussing this treaty now from the point of view of the Canadian producer. I am not objecting to giving Australia a preference, and a big preference, on such articles as raisins and currants, and of raising the tariff to do so. We have to give something to get an advantage, and it is well to choose an article where it can be given at the expense of outsiders and not at the expense of the Canadian producer himself. On the
next article, fruits in airtight cans or other airtight packages, and so forth, the present British preferential tariff is a cent and three-quarters, the general tariff two and a half cents. That cent and three-quarters was, under the first treaty, to be reduced to a cent and a quarter, but the general tariff was to be raised from two and a half to three and a quarter cents. There would be something for the Canadian fruit producer to offset partly, if not wholly, the sacrifice he was asked to make. But the government went back to Australia and said, "We will let all your fruits, dried and all the rest of them, in a half a cent, and we will keep our general tariff just where it is, two and a half cents. Honey is treated similarly, other articles the same, until of the twenty articles nine of them now come in wholly free, and on not one of them produced in Canada is the producer given a particle more advantage against any country in the world than he had before the minister went to Australia.

Now, may I ask why did the government retreat from its pledge with Australia and go back and1 ask for a new treaty? Why was the offer which they were so ready to make to reform the Petersen contract repeated in the case of a sister colony? Why was the advantage which the Canadian farmer was to get under the first treaty, partially in lieu of the sacrifice he had to make, absolutely wiped away? Will the minister explain? Has the minister, has the government attempted to explain why they retreated from the position which they took with Australia, and which they agreed with Australia they would submit to this parliament. Nine of the twenty articles now come in free. I can understand a man who adheres to the free trade doctrine -if such is left-feeling that this is all right, that the further you go in this direction the better. It is all right to get markets for our newsprint. Nobody objects to that. It is wise to do it, and it is wise to make a concession to do it; wise to get a market for our canned salmon, and wise to make a concession for it.
Does the right hon. gentleman intimate that the members of the government are enunciating a free trade doctrine?

No, except in such portions of the country as they think it is safe to do so, that is all. It is wise, I say, to make a concession to get these things, but by this treaty the government just calls on the mixed farm-er of Canada to be good enough to step up to the counter and pay the whole cost of the concessions that they have given Australia. Out of him and him alone comes the whole price, and in compensation they give him not one single concession. The minister says "Oh well, not many of these goods are coming into Canada now. We have not imported much meat or canned meat or poultry and game, so we do not need to fear the competition." Has the minister considered that though very little may come in over a three-cent tariff, very much more may come in over a half-cent tariff when applied t-o a single pound of meat?

An horn. MEMBER: From a country eight thousand miles away.

Yes, from a country eight thousand miles away, when the freight to bring it here is less than the freight over half the length of Canada; and from that country it is coming to-day.
Australia has never been getting these goods in under the British preference tariff; she has been paying the general tariff rate. The tariff Australia paid previously on meats was three cents; now it is half a cent. On canned meats it was 27| per cent; now it is 15. The tariff on lard was 2 cents; now it is free; on tallow, 20, now 10; eggs 3, now free; cheese 3, now free; butter 4, now one cent. In a word, what was a fairly substantial tariff is now virtually wiped out. So that all this argument of the Minister that because little has come under the general tariff from Australia not very much will come when there is no tariff at all -that argument is just so much casuistry, just so much guess work. We are to-day importing butter, a considerable amount, as has been stated by the minister himself, from countries just as distant as Australia, over tariffs far higher than the minister now proposes to impose.
We imported 198,341 pounds of butter last year, and we exported 24,000,000 pounds.

I know, and we imported it over a substantial tariff, not over a tariff of a cent a pound. I would like to know upon what principle of equity he makes the Canadian farmer pay the whole of this. The minister knows what he should have done just as well as he knows he is sitting in his seat to-night. He did it in respect to raisins and currants, and he started to do it on other articles too, but he got frightened, and I think I can see in front of me now the people who frightened him. He was afraid of the votes of hon. gentlemen to my left. He did not *want to carry his measure with the support of the Conservative party; he wanted to maintain up to the day of the election what.

Australian Treaty
alliance he could with the Progressive party. Now, hon. members to my left are certainly under no humiliation from that talk, but I wonder what condition the government is in? That was its purpose and that alone. The fact that they negotiated and completed a treaty with Australia, subject to parliament, along the lines that we have repeatedly advised in this parliament, certainly shows that they know that is the right line, but they had not the courage to follow it through. Even the first treaty, while it certainly was not fair to the farmer of Canada, was infinitely better than this. Under the first treaty they made him pay, but at least they gave him something in return; they gave him an increased duty against other countries. The minister knowrs what he should have done, and this government knows what it should have done, namely, to have taken our tariff on farm products and given a tariff practically on a level with the American tariff against the world, and then said to Australia: " Come in under our British preferential tariff; we will thus give you an attractive preference in our markets. We can do that and be fair to the farmer of Canada." But the government did not have the courage to do so. The government was afraid of the Progressive votes.
Afraid of the farmers.
No, afraid of the Progressives, a very different thing. But it will be afraid of the farmers when it gets amongst the farmers of Ontario and Quebec, and faces them with these duties.
Do not be afraid.

I can show the hon.
gentleman resolutions from very close to his own county against the tariff on farm products as it stands to-day; what will these farmers say when it stands where it is going to stand after this treaty passes How can a member representing a rural county go back to that county and say: "I am a supporter of protection for industry." I know the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) will say that, because I know he is. " I am a supporter," he will say, "of protection for the industries of Canada, but when it comes to you, I do not care a whit about you. I am in favour of half a cent a pound on the meats that you produce. I am in favour of fifteen per cent on your canned meats and canned poultry. I am in favour of lard, eggs and cheese coming in free. As for you, I have no concern at all; the protection I want is only for manufactured goods." Those who believe in free trade principles can uphold such a theory, but those who believe in protection will have
great difficulty in supporting any system which does not apply equitably to all portions and all classes of the producers of this country. I am not one of those who decry the benefits obtained by this treaty. I am as anxious as anybody to extend the market for Canadian produced paper, canned goods, or any other products of Canada. But we should have a tariff on a level where we could give concessions, and give them at the expense of outside competitors, not give a preference over the producers themselves of this country. Had we had such a tariff, the negotiations of a treaty with Australia would have been comparatively easy. We would then have had something to offer, something of an advantage over other countries competing with us who give us no concession. Now we have given something to Australia to the disadvantage of our own farm producers, in order that Australia may let some of our manufactured goods in at the same level at which she admits the same goods from other countries. As a matter of fact, the schedule which is the most unjust of the whole of the tariff schedules of Canada to-day is that relating to farm products. The first tariff schedule I would raise in this country is the farm product schedule; the one that I would raise most substantially of all is the tariff which applies to farm products. The farmer in this country to-day is competing with his fellow farmer in other countries under conditions of absolute unfairness. The goods which he produces are brought into this country over a relatively low tariff or none at all, while he is forbidden access to those other countries save over a tariff that he simply cannot scale.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend says we
are precluded from exporting these products to foreign countries except on the payment of high duties. What about England?

Certainly we are on a
level witlh other countries as to admission to England. We have no advantage over them, but they have a big advantage over us in admission to their own country as compared with their admission to us, and that is what I am complaining of. Speaking of England, any one who has watched the trend of events in recent months in tlhat country will find it hard to become elated over the results of the fiscal policy which they have been pursuing, and I do not think in that view I am differing very widely from the view of the minister (Mr. Beland) himself. No; it is not that I have any hostility toward trade treaties, especially with our Dominions. To them, in fact, I would extend a welcome; I would
Australian Treaty

make greater concessions to secure them than I would to secure treaties with those who are beyond the circle of empire,for the reason that they are likely to be more permanent, and I think as well that inasmuch as in many lines they produce differently from ourselves the basis for a trade treaty exists.
It is well to have these inter-dominion treaties, but we ought first to be in a position where we can make those treaties without being compelled to force our own producers to pay the whole price, instead of doing as other countries do, that is, have a tariff from which we can make concessions and be fair to our own producers at the same time. France has made a treaty with us, and a very favourable treaty for France, but France in making that treaty never for a moment sacrificed a single producer in France. We did in this country. The minister talks of the Frendh treaty being 75 per cent for the advantage of the Canadian farmer. The minister cannot name one article, not one single clause in the French treaty that is of benefit to the Canadian farmer.

How can France make
such a treaty as the right hon. gentleman speaks of in favour of France without helping the French farmer?

Without helping the
French farmer? It is helping the French farmer altogether, but I am looking after our own farmers. The Canadian farmer got nothing out of the French treaty. France has a very high tariff, and France simply said to Canada: You give us certain concessions in your country, or our highest tariff goes up against you, and Canada bent the knee and gave the concessions. In some such corresponding position Canada should be, and then we could treat with other nations without sacrificing our own producers.
I thought the right hon. gentleman said that the French farmer had not been sacrificed at all.

That is exactly what I said. The French farmer is not sacrificed in the French treaty, -but our farmer is. What about the condensed milk duties against us. They were multiplied fifty per cent over what they were before, and we were told we would have to take that or a higher tariff still would go on. We took it with the result that it killed our condensed milk export from this country to France. That is how this government helped the Canadian farmer in the French treaty.
Is it not a fact that we are put on a parity with the United States in the matter of this French treaty?

We were put on a parity for some little parts of farm implements, those manufacturers were the only people who got any 'benefit out of it. The United States gave nothing in return whatever, but we had to go and give all these concessions, and we are always going to be in that position, so long as this government pursues its present course.
Without the negotiation of the French treaty, would not the United States have been at am advantage over us in the French market?

Certainly they would
have in respect of those farm implements that some of our manufacturers were selling there. I do not say that it was not an advantage, but I ask the bon. gentleman how was it that America got that with no concessions at aM on her part, while we made very extensive concessions to get the same thing?
We got cheaper champagne.

Yes, and we lost a million, nearly two million dollars in revenue. The French treaty was an unqualified disaster for this country, and a disaster just because of the policy of this government. Now we are making further concessions because of the very same state of affairs. As long as we have a government pursuing this course, we will have to continue to do so-either that or no treaty at all. As for me, when I stand for protection, I stand for consistent protection to all '.parts of our country, and to all classes of producers. I aim' not going to stand here, no matter how strong the importunity may be, no matter whence it comes, and vote for any treaty that does an injustice to a great proportion of the producers of this country, though it does bring benefit to others. Do justice to all. France was able to do justice to all, and make an advantageous treaty. Finland was able to do the same thing. The United States to-day could do the same. But this government cannot do so with any country on earth, and it could not reveal a more conspicuous example of failure than the treaty that is before us to-night.

Is it not a fact that this
treaty is terminable at six months' notice? Does not the right hon. gentleman think it would be well to give it a trial? Probably all these troubles he foresees .may not actually occur.

Australian Treaty

I admit the terminable clause is perhaps the best the treaty contains. I am not saying there are not advantages in the treaty; there are, but you cannot defend advantages by unfairness. This treaty is not fair to the Canadian farmer. It is utterly unjust and injurious to him.
Is it not wise to give it a trial?

I desire to point out to
the Acting Minister of Finance the injustice this treaty does to the canning industry of the country. He no doubt is aware that one of the greatest industries in Ontario is the canning industry. The farmers all over Ontario, or at least the western and southern parts of Ontario, are dependent upon the canning factories to take the product of their farms. The tariff on canned goods, as the minister knows, is already too low. It is a cent and a half a pound. With reference to canned vegetables, why allow Australia to ship their canned vegetables into Canada free under this treaty? On canned fruits the
Australian Treaty

rate is half a cent a pound, while Australia puts up a tariff of eleven cents a pound. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, it is a very unreasonable and one-sided proposition. I was glad the Prime Minister stated that if he found [DOT]his treaty worked an injustice to any industry he would repeal it. My advice to him is to lock the door before the horse is stolen. What is the use of trying to save an industry after it has already gone into liquidation? I am satisfied that if this treaty is ratified a great injustice will be done to the canning industry of this country. If we allow Australia, with cheap water rates, to dump her canned fruit and canned vegetables into this country, untold damage will be done to our canning industry, and as I stated, the canning factory of Ontario is closely connected with the farmer and is of vital interest to him. If, as suggested by my right hon. leader, they had raised the duty equal to the duty going into the United States they could well afford to give Australia the preference of a cent and a half a pound which would not have worked an injustice to the canning industry of this country.

This treaty was made in September, and we tried, on more than one occasion after the opening of the House this session, to get information as to why it was not brought down, and we were told, as my leader said a few minutes ago, that the excuse of the acting minister for not bringing it down was that Australians wanted a provision that 75 per cent of all goods going there be made in Canada. I do not see anything in the treaty to bear out that information which he gave to the House. I think that when the leader of the opposition asked the minister a few minutes ago for an explanation in regard to this matter, the least he could have done was to have given some sort of explanation, but it has never been given. We have asked for information on many occasions as to the particulars of the treaty, and I find that on the 11th October in 'the government publication called the Commercial Intelligence Journal a resume was given of this Australian treaty. They were very particular in this journal to give all the advantages that Australia was giving to us. That was well advertised by the government. The government took great pains to make known all over Canada the advantages Canada was getting from this treaty. What was the reason for that? The minister told us the other day that the Manufacturers' Association and the paper people stated that the treaty suited them. Of course
fMr. Hubbs.]
they only knew one side of the treaty. They never knew the disadvantages that other industries and other businesses in this country had to suffer because of this treaty.
How does it compare with our loan to Roumania?
The hon. member for Dorchester should not complain of that, because he stated that it was an asset worth par.
Let the hon. member answer for himself.

In the Commercial Intelligence Journal the statement was made that Canada is to extend to Australia the full benefit of the British preferential tariff. That was the statement made in the government's own journal in October, and they go on to relate in this organ that they are going to give this concession on raisins which was passed last year.
What is that document?

The Commercial Intelligence Journal, published under the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Hon. Thomas A. Low, M.P., under date of October 11. That is the treaty that was passed in the Australian House, and the Prime Minister told us a few moments ago that, as regards all these further concessions we are making, because these are concessions, Australia will be kind enough to accept them. They will not refuse them. At least they have promised to pass them in the House. It is very considerate, when we give them nothing but concessions,, they are willing to accept them without refusing. We were to give Australia the full British preference. What do we find now? Meats that were to have a duty of a cent a pound, have the duty reduced now to one-half cent a pound. But under this arrangement, under the proposition that was laid down in this journal at that time, these different products were to have an increase in duty. This was the proposition that was published and which the manufacturers of this country had heard about and passed judgment upon. They never passed judgment upon this treaty, nor sent their recommendations or acceptances of this treaty to this government with any knowledge -of the present treaty. The thing is entirely different. It is not the same treaty at all. The item of canned meats is apparently one of. the things that remain the same. There is; a difference of about 2J per cent. The duty

Australian Treaty
on lard is changed from one-half cent a pound in the former treaty to free. The duty on beeswax is the same. The duty on eggs has been reduced from one cent a dozen to free, and the duty on cheese from one cent a pound to free.

Between the old treaty
and this?

Yes, but not between the
British preferential and this. It looks to me as if they had three trials at a treaty, because in the first one they speak of the British preference. They have been negotiating right along, and they probably have had a dozen treaties but they do not tell us about them. We could not get the information at the time, but we were able to get it from an American journal. The Board of Commerce reports of [DOT]October 6, six or seven days prior to the publication of this journal in a round-about way- no doubt they did not get it from this government, but they got it from somewhere else-published full details of the treaty. It comes from Australia, and this treaty as published from there is not the same as any of the others. In this particular volume they give the Australian concessions to Canada and the Canadian concessions to Australia. Our publication six or seven days later took very good care to cover up the Canadian concessions to Australia. We did not hear anything about them. They were covered up, as I stated before in the paragraph that we were to have nothing but the plain British preference. For my part, I can find no objection to that portion of the treaty that gives a preference to the fish producers or to the pulp and paper industry. But I take very strong exception to making the producers of fruits and vegetables the goat to carry the proposition for the other fellow. I want to put on record some telegrams that I have received from my constituency. I represent a riding that has twenty-five canning factories in it, and I also have paper industries. I doubt very much if there is another single constituency in Canada that has a larger paper industry than we have, I mean in volume of industry or in the spread of it. There is made in my_ riding and in the nearby constituency, kraft tissue paper, newsprint, writing paper, coated paper, papers that are waxed for carrying lard, butter and stuff of that kind. Therefore, I have both industries in my riding. I doubt very much if the paper industry, or even the fish industry, if they thought another very substantial industry in this country was going to be injured because of the benefit they were going to receive, would be so eager for this treaty to be
brought into effect if they knew the whole story. The government took very good care, in any of their publications and as regards advising parliament; not to let the people know. The public do not know anything about the matter. In fact the farmers of the country did not know. This is a telegram which I received a day or so ago from a growers' cooperative association of Jordan:
Understand Australian treaty before parliament Friday reduced duty on canned fruit from Australia to one-ha-lf cent per pound canned vegetables free desire to protest strongly against this reduction as it will seriously affect our industry and the industry of fruit ra.sing in whicli many of your constituents are vitally interested. Trust you will use every effort to combat this.
Another one from a shipper who represents 300 growers and who ships for 300 growers:
Reported proposed reduction to half cent pound in duty on Australian canned fruits and vegetables free fruit and vegetable growers now in serious financial condition and if proposed legislation goes through will without doubt cause great hardship to many growers.
I also want to read a telegram from a cooperative cold storage outfit in my city.

Before the hon. member
proceeds any further, rule 16, paragraph 202 states:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside of the House and referring to or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings in the House.
We are not interested in what the constituents of my hon. friend might think of this treaty. We are interested in his opinion. If an hon. member is to be allowed to read before this committee all the letters or expressions of opinions of his constituents concerning this piece of legislation, when will the debate end? The hon. member may give his opinion and we shall listen to it. He is welcome to speak, so far as he is concerned, as long as he wishes, but according to this rule he is out of order in reading the telegrams he is now reading.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I should like to have
an opportunity of listening to the hon. member a little further before giving a ruling.

I have heard many letters and telegrams read in this House respecting matters of a similar nature. If the hon. gentleman had not taken up as much time as he did. I would have been through. This last telegram is from the St. Catharines Cold Storage Com-nany who represent 500 shippers. They wire:
We desire enter emphatic protest against reported reduction duty on Australian fresh, canned and dried fruits as endangering the living of all Canadian fruit growers who are at present time suffering heavy losses
Australian Treaty

owing competition from United States. See car reports for arrival southern tomatoes which displace home grown hothouse tomatoes also American strawberries arriving this week Montreal and Toronto.
I do not object to the paper and the fish industries getting an advantage in the Australian market but 1 certainly object to the fruit growers and canning companies of this country having to pay for it. The acting minister (Mr. Rdbb) and the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) say that the importations will not amount to very much. Well, what did Australia make the treaty for? They are giving us some large concessions in pulp and paper and in fish. Are they doing that for nothing or do they expect some return? It is natural that they should expect something in return, and if they are to get it through shipping these canned goods in the quantities they no doubt expect to be able to send here it will do the people of this country a great deal of harm. The minister says that we are shippers of these goods ourselves. Do we not produce enough butter and eggs and other stuff of that kind in this country without giving an inducement to people outside to bring in more of it to add to competition here? Is there not competition enough in this class of -goods without encouraging more from outside? When presenting this subject the other day the minister said that the reductions he proposed to make would reduce the cost of the breakfast table without injuring any industry in Canada. Now, if he is going to make these reductions in the cost of the breakfast table in the way he proposes does he mean to tell us that the farmer will get more for his produce? If the breakfast table in Montreal and Toronto is cheapened in regard to butter and eggs will the farmer get more for these commodities which he has to sell? He may do so in Chateauguay-Huntingdon but I doubt it, and he will find this out before long. If the cost of the breakfast table is to be reduced the difference will come out of the farmer's pocket and no other.

-In view of the statement made by the minister on March 16, I think the question put to him by the leader of the opposition and by another member deserves some attention. The leader of the opposition stated with regard to the delay in bringing on the treaty that the -government of Australia after having passed their legislation had passed an order in council changing the percentage that would apply to goods coming under their tariff. Hon. -gentlemen understand that under our tariff -goods twenty-five per cent manufactured in the British

Empire are allowed the preference; and that was Changed by Australia to seventy-five per cent, so that we are negotiating with them to have this matter more clearly defined. The minister on that occasion clearly misled the House, and he ought to make some explanation in regard to the situation to-day. He cannot afford to sit in his seat and allow challenges of this kind to be thrown across the floor, and expect parliament to adopt this treaty as it has been placed -before us to-day, an entirely different treat}' from the one made with Australia in the past summer as announced -by the parliament of that dominion. Why has the change been made -and Australia given better terms than they asked for when the first treaty was agreed upon? The statement of the -minister on March 16 has not been substantiated.

My hon. friend was not in
his place a short While ago when I quoted the telegram which I have received from the commissioner to the effect that the same treatment extended to Great Britain and other British possessions will be accorded Canada.

If this was the reason
for the delay during these six months why was it not stated in the new treaty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In the couree
of his remarks my right hon. friend stated that there had been an intimation in the Speech from the Throne with regard to the Australian treaty.
And other treaties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No mention
was made of the subject.

It refers to certain
treaties.
Mr, MACKENZIE KING: I beg my right hon. friend's pardon; it has no reference to the Australian treaty. The reason was that at the time the Speech from the Throne was being written Mr. Ross, the Australian trade commissioner, was with Mr. Logan in the West Indies. The government at that time had before them considerations of which it has since taken account with respect to the final negotiations in relation to the Australian treaty, and were waiting for the return of Mr. Ross from the West Indies to send him to Australia to conclude the investigations there. We were not certain how the investigations might turn out and mention was not made of the treaty in the Speech from the Throne.

Australian Treaty

I said that it referred to certain treaties, and I will read the exact
passage:
Your attention will also be invited, during the course of the session, to certain trade agreements, to legislation respecting the handling and marketing of Canadian grain and to other important matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend spoke of the Australian treaty specifically.
I said the Australian treaty and others.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am explaining to the House now, in order that they may appreciate the reason for the delay, that the government was considering at the time certain matters which it thought necessary to take into account, and it was desirable that Mr. Ross should go to Australia to explain things in a verbal way which would have been impossible by cable. We therefore had to wait until his return from the West Indies.

Was not the question, which it was necessary to explain, the intention of the present government to give Australia better terms than they would have-got under the former treaty? The minister certainly has not justified the delay in this matter. No evidence has been submitted to show that the government ever had any intimation that Australia was going to or had passed an order in council to that effect. So far he has made no reference to the order in council which he claimed had been passed by Australia. I have listened to the Prime Minister's explanation or his justification for making this treaty, in the course of which he dilated upon the "larger vision of imperial trade." Apparently this was the impelling motive in the minds of the government when negotiating this treaty. It has been pointed out. that the balance of trade is very largely in our favour. Surely this is nothing to be regretted. We ought to be able to find profitable business somewhere in the wrorld. There are a sufficient number of obstacles in our way without adding to them. The dairy industry is very materially affected by this treaty according to the statement published in the produce market report for June 10 issued by the Department of Agriculture. It shows that Canada has been exporting butter to twenty-two countries in an endeavour to find markets, and I notice also that in the Dairy and Cold Storage branch report for June 20, 1925, the following reference is made to the' cheese market in Canada.
The final report of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics issued on the 20th inst. shows the stocks of cheese in all Canada on June 1, 1925, were 15,421,532 pounds,
as compared with a five year average on the same date of 5.805,099 poundsor three times the quantity which is usually held in cold storage at that time. But there is this rather significant comment:
The heavy increase in 'holdings is no doubt due to heavy stocks of cheese imported for the purpose of manufacturing "process" loaf cheese.
So that we are to-day importing large quantities of cheese, in fact one consignment alone of 29,452 boxes came into Montreal recently, and we have at the present time ten million pounds more cheese in cold storage in Canada than there has been on an average for the past five years. And we are asked not to be concerned about this treaty. "That it is an experiment, and if you do not like it after a while you can change it for something else, but it is the best we could do for you." It is not the best. The government had a better trade treaty with Australia six months ago, but they chose not to put it into effect. They are apparently deliberately sacrificing the primary industries of this country for some ulterior motive. So far they have not offered any justification for what they are attempting to do. But the Prime Minister states, "If you let this chance go by it may never come again." I never heard anything sound so much like a gold brick story. It is similar to what we heard when the transcontinental railway was being built. Then we were told that if we missed that, the greatest opportunity of our lives, we would forever regret it. And the Prime Minister now states, we are about to miss another opportunity if we do not allow this treaty to pass. If not, Australia may do something terrible to prevent us doing business with her. Evidently the impelling motive in the minds -of the government in pushing forward this treaty is the paper interests. The influence which has been brought to bear upon them has assuredly been from those interested in that industry. Why is it that Australia discriminates against Canada to the extent of three pounds per ton on paper? Have hon. gentleman ever asked themselves that question? Pulp and paper can be shipped from the United Kingdom into Australia free. Now the government are anxious to secure a reduction of the tariff against our puipwood, and to do so they are going to sacrifice our primary industries. The Minister of Trade and Commerce in Australia knew very well his country was getting the best of the bargain when he submitted the treaty to parliament. He realized the difficulty the Canadian government would have in convincing any sane person in this Dominion that the treaty was
Australian Treaty

I must correct the hon.
gentleman's figures. I have here the official year book of the Commonwealth of Australia, giving the figures of exports of animals from Australia for the year 1922-23, and it shows that their total export of cattle in that year was 13,318.

Then the return
published by the Australian government is not correct. The figures I have quoted are to be found in the Australian oversea trade returns. I copied them a few days ago and I am sure they are correct. The exports of sheep hides, without the wool,, amounted to 9,610,335, and of that number 139,973 were shipped into Canada in 1922-23. I am satisfied that the supporters of the government in this House do not realize the danger to which we are being subjected by a treaty of this kind. You are practically removing a very, very low tariff indeed in connection with meats, such as Australia can produce at little or no cost at all, where sheep graze all the year round, and it is simply a matter of rounding them up. The sole value of many of their flock of sheep is considered to be in the wool, and very little or no value is attached to the carcass. Now if they can find a market for their mutton and lamb in some other country, they will be only too glad to avail themselves of the opportunity.

I fear my hon. friend has
unintentionally left a wrong impression on the committee. He was giving the exports of cattle and sheep from Australia, and he quoted figures running up into the hundreds 306
of thousands. The total importations from all countries of cattle into Canady in the year ending March 31, 1925, were 214 only, and they came from the United States.

The year I gave
was 1923-24.
My hon. friend also quoted figures up in the thousands for sheep. There were no sheep imported into Canada from any other country except the United States, from which we got 1,576.

I can only reaffirm
that my figures were taken from the trade returns of the Commonwealth of Australia.
I am giving you our figures.

I was giving the
figures for the years that I mentioned. Of currants we imported 96,320 pounds in 192324 and 184,800 pounds in 1922-23.
The fact that we are asked to include in this treaty a clause which enables the government by simply passing an order in council to make similar trade arrangements with any other British country shows how far-reaching this proposal is. I have expressed my opinion regarding the treaty. I have expressed also my disappointment regarding the attitude of the government and their failure to give any reasonable explanation as to why such an agreement has been made. I am sure a great injury will be done to an industry that finds great difficulty in carrying on at the present time. Labour conditions in this country to-day are such that those engaged in agriculture are carrying on very largely short-handed, doing what little work they can, because the returns from the farm will not enable them to pay the wages which are determined by the scale that has been fixed by the government in the civil service of this country and on the railways in this country and elsewhere. The eight-hour day, and the six-hour day in many cases, is in effect, and agriculture has to compete. And now the government have signified their approval of a scheme for old age pensions in this country. We have reached the stage, Mr. Chairman, where something will have to be done. If we are going to carry on at all, labour of certain classes cannot continue to receive the consideration it has been receiving. Wages must come down in this country to a competitive basis if we have to compete with cheap production in foreign countries, speaking with regard to agriculture. People find it difficult to carry on as they could do in years gone by; this would not be possible except for improved machinery

Australian Treaty

which enables a man or a boy to do the work that it took three or four men to do a few years ago. The country has become overrun with noxious weeds.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

My hon. friends
may laugh and "ha, ha." It is a great joke, I suppose, but you can travel this country from one end to the other, and wherever you go you will see this is the case. The farmers of this country are carrying a heavy load and the government are not attempting to relieve them in the slightest but are making it more difficult for them.

I rise to a point of order,
Mr. Chairman. My point is that a discussion of noxious weeds has nothing to do with this treaty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member mentioned that only incidentally.

Anyone who has
knowledge of the rules of the House knows there was no justification for the hon. member rising to a point of order. Only one deduction can be drawn, and that is that he rose just for the purpose of interrupting.

Not at all. I shall be glad
to apologize if the hon. gentleman can show me any connection between noxious weeds in Canada and the Australian treaty.

I am saying it is
absolutely impossible for the farmers of this country to continue to carry the load they are carrying to-day. Their industry has been neglected, and as an evidence of that you can see noxious weeds flowering in this country everywhere.
Not in Quebec.

The only hope for
agriculture in this country is to develop the live stock business and put it on a profitable basis. In many sections of the country lands that were neglected and practically ruined a few years ago by grain growing have been partially reclaimed by such a process, but the government are going to make it difficult if not impossible for this to go on.
I spoke on this question yesterday, but in view of the attitude of the government, in view of the absence of any reasonable justification offered by the Prime Minister and the Acting Minister of Finance for this trade agreement, and realizing the seriousness of the situation, I have felt compelled to voice my protest against this most iniquitous measure which the government are now endeavouring to force on the country.
